item.title: AI Agent Monitoring in Claude Code: Catch Silent Failures
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: AI agent monitoring for solo builders: use Claude Code hooks, a cron wrapper and a free heartbeat check to catch silent failures without a monitoring stack.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

AI agent monitoring means tracking what an autonomous agent did, what it produced and what it cost on every run, so you find out when it fails before your users or your data do. If you are a solo builder running Claude Code on a schedule, you can skip the enterprise OpenTelemetry dashboard. A Claude Code Stop hook that checks the agent's expected output, a cron wrapper that logs total_cost_usd, and a free heartbeat check will catch most silent failures, such as a nightly aggregation that "finished" but never wrote the file.

Which option is right for you?

Start with the cheapest setup that can tell you a job failed. Add tracing only when a single log line no longer explains why it failed.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner, one scheduled Claude Code taskCron wrapper + output check + free heartbeat (Healthchecks.io Hobbyist, $0)Claude Code hooks reference
Daily work use, several recurring jobsStop/StopFailure hooks writing a JSONL run log, plus heartbeat per job/claude-code-hooks-examples-7-copy-paste-scripts/
Budget-sensitive, API-key billing--output-format json cost logging + --max-budget-usd capRun Claude Code programmatically
Want charts without running serversClaude Code OpenTelemetry export to Grafana Cloud FreeClaude Code monitoring docs
Multi-agent app built on LangGraphLangSmith Developer plan (5k traces/month free)LangChain pricing
Company with an existing Datadog or Splunk contractThat vendor's agent observability productDatadog agent monitoring blog

Why these picks: the beginner row costs nothing and catches "never ran" and "ran but produced nothing". The daily-use row adds a history you can grep. The budget row stops runaway spend at the CLI level. Each row further down adds visibility but also adds a vendor account and more setup.

What Is AI Agent Monitoring?

AI agent monitoring means recording what an agent did, produced and finished on every run. That record lets you detect errors, drift and silent failures.

Classic uptime monitoring asks whether a process is alive. Agent monitoring asks whether the work got done. Datadog's AI observability explainer frames the difference as "answering not just whether a system is running, but whether its outputs are correct, grounded, safe, and useful."

For a solo builder, a run has three things to watch:

  • Process outcome. Did claude -p exit 0? Claude Code exits with code 0 on success and a non-zero code when the run fails.
  • Work outcome. Does the artifact exist, is it fresh, and does it contain plausible data? No vendor tool knows this for you. You have to define it.
  • Cost and behavior. How much did the run spend, how many turns did it take, and did it hit an API error?

Example of a silent failure. Say a nightly job asks Claude Code to aggregate yesterday's orders into reports/daily-2026-10-22.csv. The source API returns an empty page, Claude writes a header-only CSV, explains that "no orders were found," and exits 0. Every process-level signal is green, and your weekly revenue chart quietly drops a day.

Pitfall: treating the agent's final message as the status. The model can sound confident while the file is empty. Check the file itself.

How Is AI Monitoring Different from AI Agent Monitoring?

AI monitoring is the umbrella term for watching any AI system, including models, data and outputs. AI agent monitoring narrows the focus to multi-step runs that call tools and act on their own.

AI monitoring (general)AI agent monitoring
Unit you watchA model call or predictionA whole run: prompts, tool calls, files written
Typical signalsLatency, error rate, drift, output quality scoresTask completion, tool failures, loops, retries, cost per run
Typical failureWrong or degraded answerWrong action, a skipped step, or a "success" with no output
Who usually needs itML teams serving modelsAnyone letting an agent do recurring work

Datadog's explainer describes the agent-specific part as tracing "multi-step decision chains, monitors tool selection and execution, detects agent loops and runaway behavior."

For example: if you only call the Claude API to classify support tickets, general AI monitoring (accuracy on a sample, latency, cost) is enough. Once Claude Code reads files, runs scripts and writes reports, you also need to know which step broke.

What Is a Monitoring Agent?

A monitoring agent is either collector software installed on a host, like the Datadog Agent, or an AI agent whose job is watching other agents.

The two meanings get mixed up in search results. The traditional one comes first: "The Datadog Agent is software that runs on your hosts." It collects metrics and logs and ships them to a backend, and no AI is involved.

The newer meaning is an LLM that judges another agent's work. Claude Code supports this directly. Besides shell command hooks, it has prompt and agent hook types, with default timeouts of 30 seconds and 60 seconds, against 600 seconds for command hooks (Claude Code hooks reference). A Stop hook of type prompt could ask a model whether the run really finished its task.

Pitfalls and fixes:

  • The judge is nondeterministic and costs tokens. Use deterministic shell checks first: file exists, row count, valid JSON. Add an LLM judge only for questions a script can't answer, such as "is this summary faithful to the source?"
  • The watcher fails silently too. If the monitoring agent crashes, nothing alerts you. Pair it with an external heartbeat (covered below) that expects a ping and alerts when none arrives.

Agent vs Agentless Monitoring: What's the Difference?

Agent-based monitoring installs a collector on the machine for deep, real-time data. Agentless monitoring sends or pulls data over APIs, with less setup and less detail.

Agent-basedAgentless
SetupInstall and update a daemon (e.g., Datadog Agent, OTel Collector)No daemon; push over HTTP or OTLP, or poll an API
DepthHost metrics, process data, local logsOnly what you explicitly send
MaintenanceUpgrades, config, resource use on the hostVery little
Fits solo builders?Overkill for one laptop or a $5 VPSUsually yes

The hook-based setup in this guide is agentless. Claude Code itself emits the data, either through hooks or its built-in OpenTelemetry exporter, and a curl sends a heartbeat. Claude Code's exporter can talk to a collector or straight to an OTLP endpoint. You set OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT and pick otlp, prometheus, console or none for OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER (Claude Code monitoring docs).

Pitfall: going agentless and then assuming you see host problems. A full disk or a cron daemon that died won't show up in Claude Code's telemetry because Claude Code never starts. Fix: the external heartbeat catches "nothing ran at all", which is exactly the gap agentless setups leave.

Single Agent vs Multi-Agent: Which Needs More Monitoring?

Multi-agent systems need more monitoring, because failures often happen at handoffs between agents. A single agent can be watched with one end-of-run check.

Single agent (one claude -p run)Multi-agent (subagents, agent teams, LangGraph)
Where failures hideFinal output, tool errorsHandoffs, a subagent's partial result, shared state
Minimum signalStop hook + exit code + artifact checkPer-agent completion events + a trace that links them
Claude Code hookStopSubagentStop as well ("When a subagent finishes")
Cost riskOne context windowAgent teams use "approximately 7x more tokens than standard sessions" when teammates run in plan mode

Inside Claude Code, SubagentStop receives the same fields as Stop, including last_assistant_message (hooks reference). In headless runs, --output-format stream-json tags each subagent message with parent_tool_use_id, so you can tell which subagent said what (headless docs).

Outside Claude Code, LangGraph apps send traces to LangSmith when the LangSmith environment variables are set. In the subagent tracing docs, you filter by the lc_agent_name metadata key. The vendor-neutral standard is OpenTelemetry's GenAI agent spans, such as invoke_agent and execute_tool. The spec is still marked "Development", so attribute names can change.

Example: a research subagent returns "no sources found" and the writer subagent drafts an article anyway. A SubagentStop hook that logs each subagent's last message would show the empty handoff in your run log. Model choice per role also matters for cost. See /claude-code-subagents-model-selection-role-by-role-table/.

How Do You Track AI Agent Costs?

To track AI agent costs, log total_cost_usd from each claude -p --output-format json run and add the numbers up per job.

With --output-format json, Claude Code's response "includes total_cost_usd and a per-model cost breakdown." The docs also warn that "Both figures are client-side estimates and can differ from your actual bill." For a baseline, Anthropic reports that across enterprise deployments "the average cost is around $13 per developer per active day," with 90% of users under $30 per active day (as of October 2026; check the official page). One unattended job should cost a small fraction of that. If it doesn't, investigate.

Steps:

  1. Run your job with --output-format json and pipe the output through jq -r '.total_cost_usd'.
  2. Append one CSV line per run: date, job name, exit code, cost.
  3. Add a hard cap with --max-budget-usd (a documented CLI flag). For example, --max-budget-usd 2 for a job that normally costs $0.30. If the run hits the cap, Claude Code also stops any remaining background work (headless docs).
  4. Once a week, sort the CSV by cost. A job whose cost doubles with no change in input is usually looping or retrying.
  5. For authoritative numbers on API billing, use the Usage page in the Claude Console.

If you use a Pro or Max subscription instead of an API key, the dollar figure isn't your bill. The /usage docs say "Claude Max and Pro subscribers have usage included in their subscription." On those plans, check /usage for plan usage rather than relying on the dollar estimate (costs docs). For a full walkthrough, see /claude-code-how-to-see-token-usage-and-reduce-it/.

Pitfall: --continue and --resume report the whole conversation's total, earlier runs included (headless docs). Summing those values double-counts. Start each scheduled job as a fresh session, or log only the difference.

Which AI Agent Monitoring Tools Fit a Solo Builder?

For one person, a free heartbeat service plus Claude Code hooks covers most needs. Enterprise suites like Datadog, Splunk and AppDynamics make sense mainly if you already pay for them.

ToolWhat it does for agentsCost (as of October 2026; check the official page)Not forLimitation
Claude Code hooks + a log fileRun-level checks, JSONL history$0Teams needing shared dashboardsYou write and maintain the checks
Healthchecks.ioAlerts when a job doesn't ping or pings /failHobbyist $0 for 20 jobs, 100 log entries per job; Business $20/monthAnyone who needs tracesKnows only "pinged or not"; no detail on why
Grafana CloudCharts for Claude Code OTel metricsFree: 10k active series, 50 GB logs, 14-day retention, 3 usersPeople who don't want to build dashboardsYou design panels and alerts yourself
LangSmithStep-by-step traces for LangGraph/LangChain appsDeveloper $0, 1 seat, 5k base traces/month; Plus $39/seat/monthPure Claude Code CLI jobsBest fit only inside the LangChain ecosystem
Datadog Agent ObservabilityGraph of tools, handoffs, retries and errorsNot listed publicly for this product; contact salesSolo builders without a Datadog accountFramework mapping centers on LangGraph, CrewAI, OpenAI Agents SDK
Splunk AI Agent MonitoringPerformance, quality, tokens, estimated costEnterprise pricingSmall teamsSplunk says it "is scheduled for deprecation" in favor of Splunk Agent Observability
AppDynamics AI Agent MonitoringDashboard for LLM app performance and usageEnterprise pricingAnyone without on-prem AppDynamicsRequires Python Agent and Events Service 25.10.0 or higher

Datadog describes its product as one that "displays each step in a multi-agent workflow, including which tools agents used, handoffs between agents, retries, and errors." That level of detail helps when ten services call each other. It is more than one cron job needs.

Pitfall: buying a tracing product to fix a problem that is really "the job didn't run." Traces can't show a run that never started. A heartbeat can.

What Should an AI Agent Monitoring Dashboard Show?

A useful dashboard shows each run's status, whether the expected output passed its check, the cost, the duration and the last error. For one builder, that can be a log file.

The minimum fields per run:

FieldSource
Time, job nameYour wrapper script
Exit code$? after claude -p
Output check (pass/fail + reason)Your Stop hook or wrapper
stop_reasonStop hook input: end_turn, max_tokens, stop_sequence or tool_use (hooks reference)
API error typeStopFailure hook matcher values such as rate_limit, overloaded, billing_error
Costtotal_cost_usd

Two ways to view it:

  1. No-server option. Run jq -s 'group_by(.status) | map({status: .[0].status, n: length})' ~/.claude/monitor/runs.jsonl for a status count, and check the Healthchecks.io check list for up/down per job.
  2. Charts option. Export Claude Code telemetry with CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1, OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER=otlp and OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT set to the OTLP endpoint of your Grafana Cloud stack or collector. Then chart claude_code.cost.usage (USD) and claude_code.token.usage (tokens). Metrics export every 60 seconds by default and logs every 5 seconds (monitoring docs).

Pitfall: OTel metrics show spend and activity, not whether your CSV has rows. Keep the output check in your own log even if you add Grafana.

How Do You Build Lightweight Monitoring with Claude Code Hooks?

Use a Stop hook to check the output, and a cron wrapper to report results to a heartbeat. The hook confirms that the run's output exists and looks complete. The whole setup needs no monitoring stack.

The relevant behavior from the hooks reference: Stop fires "When Claude finishes responding," and "Stop hooks can block Claude from stopping and force the conversation to continue." Exiting with code 2 from a Stop hook prevents Claude from stopping. StopFailure fires "When the turn ends due to an API error". Its output is ignored, but the command still runs, so it can write a log line. For every event, see /claude-code-hooks-lifecycle-every-event-explained/.

Step 1: Write the Stop hook

Run mkdir -p ~/.claude/hooks ~/.claude/monitor and save the script below as ~/.claude/hooks/check-output.sh. It's an example; change the thresholds to fit your job.

#!/bin/bash
# Example Stop hook: verify the job's artifact; log every result.
input=$(cat)
session=$(echo "$input" | jq -r '.session_id')
reason=$(echo "$input" | jq -r '.stop_reason')
LOG="$HOME/.claude/monitor/runs.jsonl"
status="ok"; detail=""

# Only check when the cron wrapper set an expected file
if [ -n "$MONITOR_EXPECTED_FILE" ]; then
  f="$MONITOR_EXPECTED_FILE"
  min="${MONITOR_MIN_LINES:-2}"
  if [ ! -s "$f" ]; then
    status="fail"; detail="missing or empty: $f"
  elif [ "$(wc -l < "$f")" -lt "$min" ]; then
    status="fail"; detail="fewer than $min lines: $f"
  elif [ -n "$(find "$f" -mmin +"${MONITOR_MAX_AGE_MIN:-90}")" ]; then
    status="fail"; detail="stale file: $f"
  fi
fi

jq -nc --arg t "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)" --arg s "$session" --arg r "$reason" \
  --arg st "$status" --arg d "$detail" \
  '{time:$t, session:$s, stop_reason:$r, status:$st, detail:$d}' >> "$LOG"

# Give Claude one more attempt per session, then let it stop
marker="$HOME/.claude/monitor/retried-$session"
if [ "$status" = "fail" ] && [ ! -f "$marker" ]; then
  touch "$marker"
  echo "Output check failed ($detail). Re-check the source data and write the file, or explain exactly why it cannot be written." >&2
  exit 2
fi
exit 0

Make it executable with chmod +x ~/.claude/hooks/check-output.sh. The header-only CSV from the earlier example has one line, so MONITOR_MIN_LINES=2 flags it.

Step 2: Add a StopFailure logger

Save this as ~/.claude/hooks/log-failure.sh and run chmod +x on it as well:

#!/bin/bash
input=$(cat)
echo "$input" | jq -c '{time: (now|todate), event: .hook_event_name, session: .session_id, error: .error}' \
  >> "$HOME/.claude/monitor/runs.jsonl"

If the log shows rate_limit entries, set up retries as described in /claude-code-rate-limit-reached-retry-setup-for-cron-jobs/.

Step 3: Register both hooks

Add this to ~/.claude/settings.json (all projects) or .claude/settings.json (one project):

{
  "hooks": {
    "Stop": [
      { "hooks": [ { "type": "command", "command": "~/.claude/hooks/check-output.sh" } ] }
    ],
    "StopFailure": [
      { "hooks": [ { "type": "command", "command": "~/.claude/hooks/log-failure.sh" } ] }
    ]
  }
}

Open Claude Code and type /hooks. The docs describe it as "a read-only browser for your configured hooks." Confirm that both hooks appear under Stop and StopFailure, labeled with the right settings source.

Step 4: Wrap the job and add a heartbeat

Create a free check on Healthchecks.io and copy its ping URL. Healthchecks explains why you should report failures directly: "Actively signaling a failure minimizes the delay from your monitored service failing to you receiving an alert." The /start endpoint also lets it measure run time.

#!/bin/bash
# Example wrapper: ~/jobs/daily-orders.sh
export MONITOR_EXPECTED_FILE="$HOME/reports/daily-$(date +%F).csv"
export MONITOR_MIN_LINES=2
HC="https://hc-ping.com/YOUR-UUID"

curl -fsS -m 10 --retry 3 "$HC/start" > /dev/null
out=$(claude -p "Aggregate yesterday's orders into $MONITOR_EXPECTED_FILE" \
  --output-format json --max-budget-usd 2 \
  --allowedTools "Read,Write,Bash(python3 *)")
code=$?
cost=$(echo "$out" | jq -r '.total_cost_usd // 0')
echo "$(date -u +%FT%TZ),daily-orders,$code,$cost" >> "$HOME/.claude/monitor/costs.csv"

# Ground truth, independent of the agent and the hook
if [ "$code" -ne 0 ] || [ "$(wc -l < "$MONITOR_EXPECTED_FILE" 2>/dev/null || echo 0)" -lt 2 ]; then
  curl -fsS -m 10 --retry 3 "$HC/fail" > /dev/null
  exit 1
fi
curl -fsS -m 10 --retry 3 "$HC" > /dev/null

Schedule it with cron as shown in /claude-code-cron-job-setup-run-automations-overnight/. Now there are three layers. The hook gives Claude one chance to fix the output. The wrapper checks the file again on its own. The heartbeat alerts you if the wrapper never runs at all.

Common mistakes and fixes

  • Running with --bare, so the hooks never fire. Bare mode skips "auto-discovery of hooks" (headless docs). Fix: pass the hooks with --settings <file>, or drop --bare for this job.
  • The hook reads the transcript to find the final message. The transcript "may lag the in-memory conversation" (hooks reference). Fix: use last_assistant_message from the Stop input.
  • Network calls in a SessionEnd hook get cut off. SessionEnd hooks share a 1.5-second budget by default (hooks reference). Fix: send pings from the wrapper, not from SessionEnd.
  • The check fires during interactive coding. Stop fires after every response. Fix: the script only checks when MONITOR_EXPECTED_FILE is set, and only the cron wrapper sets it.
  • Endless blocking. A Stop hook that always exits 2 keeps Claude working. Fix: the per-session marker file allows one retry. For jobs that stall in other ways, see /claude-code-stuck-on-compacting-conversation-cron-watchdog/.
  • Untrusted project hooks in -p mode. A -p session runs the hooks in a project's .claude/settings.json "even in a folder you've never trusted." Fix: keep monitoring hooks in your own ~/.claude/settings.json and review any repo's hooks before you schedule it.

Next steps

Things you can do today:

  1. Choose the one recurring Claude Code job whose failure would hurt most. Write down the file it must produce and the minimum number of rows that output should have.
  2. Install the Stop hook and the wrapper above, run the job once by hand, then check ~/.claude/monitor/runs.jsonl and costs.csv.
  3. Test the alert: point MONITOR_EXPECTED_FILE at a path that doesn't exist and confirm that Healthchecks.io marks the check as failed.

If you'd rather not build it yourself: Healthchecks.io Business ($20/month as of October 2026; check the official page) adds capacity beyond the free 20 jobs. It suits people with many cron jobs. If you need to see inside a run, it won't help. LangSmith Plus ($39/seat/month) suits LangGraph apps that need step traces, and it adds little for plain claude -p jobs. Datadog or Splunk agent observability is worth it if your company already pays for the platform. For one person it is usually overpriced and more complex than the problem.

  • /claude-code-hooks-examples-7-copy-paste-scripts/
  • /why-claude-code-stops-mid-automation-and-how-to-fix-it/
  • /claude-code-permissions-best-practices-headless-template/

FAQ

What is AI agent studio monitoring and evaluation?

The phrase refers to the monitoring and evaluation features built into agent-building platforms. Monitoring watches live runs: errors, latency, cost. Evaluation scores outputs against test cases or rubrics. Splunk, for example, now points users to Splunk Agent Observability "to monitor, evaluate, and configure guardrails" for agentic apps. For a Claude Code job, your output check is a small evaluation that runs on every execution.

Do I need a monitoring platform for a single Claude Code agent?

Usually not. One Stop hook, a wrapper that checks the exit code and the output file, and a free heartbeat cover "didn't run", "failed" and "ran but produced nothing". Add a platform once you have several agents passing work to each other, or once teammates need a shared view.

How much does AI agent cost monitoring cost to run?

The DIY version costs nothing beyond your normal Claude usage: Healthchecks.io Hobbyist and Grafana Cloud Free are both $0 (as of October 2026; check the official pages). Hosted tracing starts at LangSmith Plus, $39 per seat per month. Datadog doesn't publish a public price for its agent product, so contact sales.

Can Splunk or AppDynamics monitor custom AI agents out of the box?

Only partly. Splunk's AI Agent Monitoring relies on OpenTelemetry GenAI instrumentation and is scheduled for deprecation. AppDynamics needs Python Agent 25.10.0 or higher configured to publish LLM events (AppDynamics docs). A Claude Code CLI job isn't a Python app, so its OTel export is the closer fit.

item.title: Claude Code Headless Mode: Flags, Auth and Cost (2026)
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: Claude Code headless mode explained: the -p flags, output formats, API key vs setup-token auth, and cost caps you need for unattended cron and CI runs.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

Claude Code headless mode means running Claude Code with no one at the keyboard. You call claude -p "your task", it does the work, prints a result and exits, the same way any shell command does. The official docs put it this way: "Add the -p (or --print) flag to any claude command to run it non-interactively" (Claude Code docs: Run Claude Code programmatically). The -p flag alone isn't enough for a reliable cron or CI job, though. You also need credentials that never ask for a browser login, permission settings that never wait for a human, a hard stop on turns and spend, and output your script can parse. This guide covers each of those.

Which option is right for you?

Use local claude -p with an API key for cron jobs on your own machine or server. Use the GitHub Action for anything triggered by repository events. Use a subscription token only for light personal automation.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner, trying one scheduled task on a laptopclaude -p with your existing Pro/Max login, no --bareRun Claude Code programmatically
Daily work: nightly cron on a VPS or home serverclaude --bare -p + ANTHROPIC_API_KEY + --max-budget-usdCLI reference
PR reviews, issue triage, scheduled repo reportsanthropics/claude-code-action@v1 in GitHub ActionsClaude Code GitHub Actions
Tight budget, already paying for Pro or Maxclaude setup-token → CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN (not with --bare)Authentication
Shared repos or a team secretConsole API key stored as an org-level secretAuthentication

The reasoning in one line each:

  • Beginner: you already have a login on the machine, so you can test the idea before you set up any billing.
  • Daily cron: an API key behaves the same on every run, and bare mode keeps stray local config out of the job.
  • GitHub events: the Action handles checkout, secrets and posting comments for you.
  • Budget: the token draws from your subscription instead of per-token billing.
  • Team: the GitHub Actions docs recommend an API key for shared secrets, because an OAuth token is tied to one person's subscription (GitHub Actions docs).

What is Claude Code headless mode?

Claude Code headless mode is the non-interactive way to run Claude Code. There's no terminal UI and no prompts. Each run takes one task, prints the result and exits. It is the same agent with the same tools as the interactive app, but it runs inside a different execution context, and that context has its own rules.

The docs describe it as the Agent SDK "available as a CLI for scripts and CI/CD" (headless docs). Several behaviors change when you add -p:

  • Permissions. With Claude Code v2.1.302 or later, claude -p runs start in Manual mode when nothing sets a permission mode. Any call that needs approval is denied unless an allow rule, a hook or a permission tool approves it (headless docs). Your job won't hang waiting for a "yes", but it may quietly fail to do the work.
  • Credentials. In -p mode an ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in the environment "is always used when present". Interactive sessions ask you first (Authentication docs).
  • Exit codes. Claude Code "exits with code 0 on success and a non-zero code when the run fails". Some failures, such as missing authentication, are printed as the result on stdout (headless docs).
  • Slash commands. Skills and custom commands still work. Terminal-only commands such as /login do not.
  • Workspace trust. Without --bare, a -p session runs the hooks in a project's .claude/settings.json and connects its .mcp.json servers "even in a folder you've never trusted" (headless docs).

That last point is the one people most often miss. If your cron job runs claude -p inside a repository you cloned from someone else, that repository's hooks will run. Bare mode prevents this.

Bare mode is the "real" headless mode

--bare skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and CLAUDE.md, so every machine produces the same result. The docs say plainly that "--bare is the recommended mode for scripted and SDK calls, and will become the default for -p in a future release" (headless docs). If you need any of that context, pass it in explicitly: --append-system-prompt-file for instructions, --settings for settings, --mcp-config for MCP servers, --agents for subagents.

The limitation: bare mode never reads OAuth credentials or the keychain. That rules out your subscription login (more on this in the auth section).

How do you run Claude Code in headless mode?

Run claude -p with a non-interactive credential, explicit tool permissions, turn and budget caps, and JSON output. Here is the sequence for a cron job on Linux or macOS.

  1. Install and check the version. Run claude --version. Several flags below need recent builds: --permission-prompts needs v2.1.259 or later, and the Manual-mode default for -p needs v2.1.302 (CLI reference). Update with claude update.
  2. Create an API key. In the Claude Console, create a key. Save it in a file only your user can read, for example ~/.config/claude-cron.env with chmod 600.
  3. Confirm auth works. Run claude auth status. It prints JSON, and authMethod should read api_key (or oauth_token if you use a subscription token). It "Exits with code 0 if logged in, 1 if not" (CLI reference).
  4. Do a dry run by hand. From the project directory:

``bash claude --bare -p "List the TODO comments in src/ and group them by file" \ --allowedTools "Read,Grep,Glob" \ --max-turns 10 \ --output-format json | jq -r '.result' ``

  1. Wrap it in a script (example):

``bash #!/usr/bin/env bash set -euo pipefail source ~/.config/claude-cron.env # exports ANTHROPIC_API_KEY cd /home/you/projects/my-app mkdir -p logs /home/you/.local/bin/claude --bare -p "Run the test suite and fix failing tests in src/ only" \ --allowedTools "Read,Edit,Bash(npm test *)" \ --permission-mode dontAsk \ --max-turns 20 \ --max-budget-usd 3.00 \ --output-format json > "logs/run-$(date +%F).json" ``

  1. Schedule it. Run crontab -e and add a line such as 0 3 * /home/you/bin/nightly-claude.sh >> /home/you/logs/cron.log 2>&1. For scheduling details and overnight patterns, see Claude Code Cron Job Setup: Run Automations Overnight.

Common mistakes and fixes

  • claude: command not found under cron. Cron uses a minimal PATH. Fix: call the absolute path from which claude.
  • The job "succeeds" but nothing changed. In Manual mode, unlisted tools that need approval are denied. Fix: add the exact tools to --allowedTools, or read permission_denials in the result (see monitoring below).
  • "Not logged in" only under cron. Your interactive login lives in the macOS Keychain or ~/.claude/.credentials.json (Authentication docs), and --bare ignores both. Fix: export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in the script.
  • The run hangs for minutes after finishing. A -p run can wait for background work. By default it stops idle background tasks after 10 minutes, and you can change that with CLAUDE_CODE_PRINT_BG_WAIT_CEILING_MS (headless docs). Also see Why Claude Code Stops Mid-Automation (and How to Fix It).
  • Piping a huge log. Piped stdin is capped at 10MB. Above that, Claude Code exits non-zero, so write the content to a file and reference the path instead (headless docs).

Which Claude Code CLI flags matter in headless mode?

Besides -p, six flags matter most: --bare, --output-format, --allowedTools, --permission-mode, --max-turns and --max-budget-usd. They decide whether a headless run is safe and parseable, and everything else is optional tuning. All of the following come from the CLI reference as of October 2026.

FlagWhat it does in a headless runDefault / note
-p, --printNon-interactive run, then exitRequired
--bareSkips hooks, skills, plugins, MCP, CLAUDE.md discoveryOff today; planned default for -p
--output-formattext, json, or stream-jsontext
--json-schemaValidated structured output in structured_outputPrint mode only
--allowedToolsTools that run without approval, e.g. "Bash(git diff *)"Uses permission rule syntax
--disallowedToolsDeny rules; a bare name removes the tool entirely"mcp__*" removes all MCP tools
--permission-modedefault/manual, acceptEdits, plan, auto, dontAsk, bypassPermissionsManual for -p (v2.1.302+)
--permission-prompts noneDenies anything that would prompt; tells Claude not to retryv2.1.259+
--max-turnsCaps agentic turns; "Exits with an error when the limit is reached""No limit by default"
--max-budget-usdStops once estimated spend hits the capPrint mode only; spend can pass the cap
--model / --fallback-modelPick a model; fall back when overloadede.g. --model sonnet
--no-session-persistenceDon't save the session to diskPrint mode only
--continue / --resume <id>Chain several -p calls into one conversationUse session_id from JSON

A few of these have traps:

  • **The space in Bash(git diff *) matters.** The docs warn that without it, Bash(git diff*) "would also match git diff-index" (headless docs).
  • --max-turns exits non-zero when it hits the cap. Your wrapper should treat that as "incomplete", not "crashed".
  • --max-budget-usd is a soft ceiling. It is checked against a client-side estimate, and "Spend can pass the cap, so leave headroom" (CLI reference).
  • bypassPermissions (--dangerously-skip-permissions) needs isolation. The docs say to "Only use this mode in isolated environments like containers, VMs, or dev containers without internet access" (Permission modes). On a personal server that has your SSH keys, prefer dontAsk with a narrow allow list. For a ready-made allow/deny set, see Claude Code Permissions Best Practices: Headless Template.

What is headless/CI mode in Claude Code?

Headless/CI mode is claude -p running inside a CI pipeline, usually via the official GitHub Action or a GitLab CI job. The pipeline supplies the credentials, the checkout and the trigger. Claude Code has no separate "CI mode" switch. In CI the runner is disposable and shared, so reproducibility and secret handling matter more than they do on your own machine.

The Claude Code GitHub Action (anthropics/claude-code-action@v1) has two modes:

  • Interactive mode. No prompt input. Claude waits for an @claude mention in an issue or PR.
  • Automation mode. You set a prompt input and Claude runs on any GitHub event, including a cron schedule.

The fastest setup is to run /install-github-app inside Claude Code. It installs the GitHub App, saves your secret as ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN, and opens a pull request with the workflow. You need admin access to the repository, and the command works only for github.com repositories (GitHub Actions docs).

Example scheduled workflow, adapted from the official daily-report example:

name: Nightly triage
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 9 * * *"
jobs:
  triage:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    permissions:
      contents: read
      issues: read
      id-token: write
    steps:
      - uses: anthropics/claude-code-action@v1
        with:
          anthropic_api_key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
          prompt: "Summarize yesterday's commits and open issues"
          claude_args: |
            --model sonnet
            --max-turns 8
            --allowedTools "mcp__github__list_commits,mcp__github__list_issues"

CI-specific pitfalls from the official docs:

  • No tools by default. With a plain-text prompt, "Claude has no shell or GitHub API access until you grant the tools the prompt needs" (GitHub Actions docs).
  • Schedules can stop on their own. GitHub runs scheduled workflows only from the default branch. In public repos it disables the schedule after 60 days without repository activity (GitHub Actions docs).
  • Fork PRs get no secrets. GitHub withholds secrets from fork pull requests on public repos, so reviews run only on same-repo branches (GitHub Actions docs).
  • Claude's commits don't trigger your CI. That happens if you pass the default GITHUB_TOKEN. Remove it so the Action authenticates as the Claude GitHub App (GitHub Actions docs).
  • Old workflows. Workflows that still reference @beta should move to @v1, with max_turns and model moved into claude_args.

How do you authenticate Claude Code for cron and CI runs?

Use an environment variable, either ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (Console billing) or CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN (subscription). Never rely on an interactive browser login, because a cron job has no browser to finish it.

When more than one credential is present, Claude Code checks them in this order (Authentication docs):

  1. Cloud provider variables (CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK, _VERTEX, _FOUNDRY)
  2. ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, used for LLM gateways
  3. ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
  4. apiKeyHelper script output, for rotating keys from a vault
  5. CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN
  6. Anthropic profile / federation credentials
  7. Subscription login from /login

Option A: API key (recommended for unattended work)

  1. Create a key in the Claude Console.
  2. Export it in your job's environment, or store it as a CI secret.
  3. Works with --bare.

When you first authenticate with Console, a workspace called "Claude Code" is created automatically. You can set spend limits on it (Costs docs).

Option B: subscription token

  1. On a machine with a browser, run claude setup-token and approve access.
  2. Copy the printed token. The command "does not save the token anywhere".
  3. Set export CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN=your-token in the job's environment.

The token lasts one year and is meant for "CI pipelines and scripts where browser login isn't available". It requires a Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise plan (Authentication docs).

Pitfalls with fixes:

  • Bare mode ignores this token. "Bare mode does not read CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN" (Authentication docs). If you want --bare, you need option A.
  • A forgotten API key silently wins. If ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set anywhere in the job's environment, it beats your subscription token and you get API charges. Run unset ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in subscription-billed scripts.
  • The token can only make model requests. It can't fetch claude.ai connectors or start Remote Control. Locally configured MCP servers still work.
  • A year passes faster than you think. Put a calendar reminder 11 months out to regenerate it.

How much does Claude Code headless mode cost?

Claude Code headless mode costs exactly what interactive use costs for the same tokens. You pay per token on an API key, or the usage comes out of your plan's limits on a subscription. There is no headless surcharge. What makes it expensive is repetition: a job that runs nightly, retries on failure, or has no turn cap can multiply spend without anyone noticing.

Official numbers (as of October 2026; check the official page):

ItemPriceSource
Opus 5.5$4 input / $20 output per million tokensClaude API pricing
Sonnet 5.5$2 input / $10 output per million tokensClaude API pricing
Haiku 5.5$0.10–$0.50 input / $0.50–$2.50 output per million tokens, depending on prompt lengthClaude API pricing
Pro plan$20/month ($17/month billed annually)Claude pricing
Max plansfrom $100/monthClaude pricing
Enterprise average~$13 per developer per active day; $150–250 per monthCosts docs

Model choice matters a lot here. Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise and the Anthropic API all default to Opus 5.5 (Model configuration), so a headless job without --model runs on the most expensive of the three. The Costs docs note that Sonnet "handles most coding tasks well and costs less than Opus".

Example estimate (illustrative, not a measurement). Suppose a nightly job reads 200,000 input tokens and writes 20,000 output tokens on Sonnet 5.5, ignoring caching. That's 0.2 × $2 + 0.02 × $10 = $0.60 per run, or about $18 for 30 nights. The same job on Opus 5.5 would be about $1.20 per run. Prompt caching usually lowers the input side, so treat this as an upper-bound sketch.

Cost controls that actually apply to headless runs:

  • --max-budget-usd 2.00 on every scheduled call
  • --max-turns sized to the task (5–10 for a report, 20+ for fix-and-test loops)
  • --model sonnet, or haiku for summarize-only jobs
  • Workspace spend limits in the Console for an API key
  • In GitHub Actions, workflow timeout-minutes and concurrency limits. Runners also bill GitHub Actions minutes on top of tokens (GitHub Actions docs)

For more ways to cut token use, see Claude Code: How to See Token Usage (and Reduce It).

Does Claude Code headless mode work with a Pro or Max subscription?

Yes. Claude Code headless mode works on Pro and Max through claude setup-token. Every automated run then draws from the same limits as your chat and interactive coding. Anthropic's help center says the limits "are shared across Claude and Claude Code", and both plans have "a five-hour session limit and a weekly limit" (Claude Help Center).

Subscription token (CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN)API key (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY)
BillingIncluded plan usagePer token, pay as you go
Works with --bareNoYes
Hits limits5-hour session and weekly windows, shared with your chatsOrganization rate limits
Good forA few light personal jobsNightly jobs, CI, anything shared
Shared team secretNot recommended (tied to one person)Recommended
Spend capPlan limits; optional usage-credit spend limit--max-budget-usd plus Console workspace limits

How to choose:

  • Pick the subscription token if you run one or two small jobs a day and want a fixed monthly bill. The limitation: a heavy overnight job can use up your session window, and you hit "You've hit your session limit" the next morning when you sit down to work interactively.
  • Pick the API key if the job matters to someone else, runs in CI, or runs often. It is not the right choice if you need a guaranteed fixed monthly cost, because per-token billing varies with the work.

When a scheduled job hits a limit, retry logic matters more than the plan. See Claude Code Rate Limit Reached: Retry Setup for Cron Jobs. In stream-json output, retries show up as system/api_retry events, with an error field such as rate_limit or billing_error (headless docs).

How do hooks work in Claude Code headless runs?

Claude Code hooks run in headless -p runs the same way they do in interactive sessions, unless you pass --bare, which skips hook discovery. That makes hooks the main way to add guardrails and logging to a job nobody watches.

The events most useful for unattended runs, per the hooks reference:

  • PreToolUse. Exit code 2 blocks the tool call. Use it to refuse rm -rf or pushes to main.
  • PermissionRequest. Can allow or deny on the user's behalf through hookSpecificOutput.decision.behavior. In a -p run this is one of the few things that can approve a call Manual mode would otherwise deny.
  • Stop. Fires when Claude finishes responding. Good for "did the tests actually pass?" checks.
  • SessionEnd. Fires when a session terminates and is meant for cleanup and logging. It also runs when you stop a -p run with SIGTERM, which exits with code 143 (headless docs).

Steps to attach a hook to a headless job:

  1. Write the hook command into a settings file, for example ci-settings.json, under "hooks": { "PreToolUse": [...] }.
  2. Without bare mode, put it in the project's .claude/settings.json. With --bare, pass it explicitly: --settings ./ci-settings.json (the documented way to load settings in bare mode).
  3. Add --output-format stream-json --verbose --include-hook-events to a test run, and confirm that hook_started / hook_response events appear.
  4. Keep hooks fast. The docs' cost example uses a PreToolUse hook to rewrite test commands so only failures reach Claude, cutting context "from tens of thousands of tokens to hundreds" (Costs docs).

Ready-made scripts are in Claude Code Hooks Examples: 7 Copy-Paste Scripts, and event order is covered in Claude Code Hooks Lifecycle: Every Event, Explained.

How do you track Claude Code usage from cron jobs?

Track Claude Code usage from cron jobs by saving the --output-format json result of every run. Each one includes total_cost_usd, a per-model cost breakdown and the session_id. Unattended runs have no screen, so if you don't log this, nobody sees it.

Example log line extraction (illustrative):

jq -c '{date: now|todate, session: .session_id, cost: .total_cost_usd, ok: (.is_error|not)}' \
  logs/run-$(date +%F).json >> logs/costs.jsonl

The session_id, result and total_cost_usd fields are documented. For any other field name (such as is_error above), check one real output file before you depend on it.

What to watch:

  • Cost per run. The docs say "Both figures are client-side estimates and can differ from your actual bill" (headless docs). For billing truth, use the Console usage page.
  • Resumed conversations. With --continue or --resume, the reported total includes earlier runs' spend. Store per-run differences, or you'll double count.
  • Silent permission failures. In stream-json, denials appear as permission_denied messages, and the final result lists them in permission_denials. A non-empty list on a "successful" run means the job didn't do what you think.
  • MCP servers that never loaded. The system/init event carries mcp_server_errors, and the docs suggest a CI gate "can fail on a non-empty array" (headless docs).
  • Missing structured output. If you use --json-schema, check that structured_output exists before using it. It is absent when Claude declines.

To get alerts when something breaks rather than just a log, see AI Agent Monitoring in Claude Code: Catch Silent Failures.

Next steps

Do today:

  1. Run claude --version and claude auth status. Confirm you're on v2.1.302 or later and see which authMethod your scripts would actually use.
  2. Take one task you do by hand every week and run it once as claude --bare -p "..." --allowedTools "Read" --max-turns 10 --max-budget-usd 1 --output-format json. Read the JSON before you schedule anything.
  3. Add --model sonnet and a --max-budget-usd cap to every existing scheduled call that lacks them.

If you'd rather not build this yourself: Anthropic's Code Review gives you automatic PR reviews "without writing a workflow", and the Claude Code GitHub Action covers scheduled repo tasks with a one-command setup (/install-github-app). Both run on your API key or subscription. The Action also uses GitHub Actions minutes. They suit people whose recurring work lives in GitHub. They don't fit jobs that touch local files, private servers or non-GitHub data, where a local cron script is still simpler. If what holds you back is subscription limits rather than setup, a Max plan (from $100/month as of October 2026; check claude.com/pricing) raises the ceiling. It is only worth it if you also use Claude Code interactively most days. For automation alone, pay-as-you-go API billing is usually easier to cap.

Related guides on this site:

  • Claude Code Cron Job Setup: Run Automations Overnight
  • Claude Code Permissions Best Practices: Headless Template
  • AI Agent Guardrails Example: Copy-Paste Claude Code Rules
  • Claude Code Stuck on Compacting Conversation: Cron Watchdog

FAQ

Can Claude Code run headless?

Yes. Claude Code runs headless with claude -p "task", which runs the full agent without the terminal UI and exits when done. It works on macOS, Linux and Windows, in cron, systemd timers, Docker and CI runners. For repeatable results, add --bare and authenticate with ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.

What is the code for headless mode?

The minimal command is claude -p "your prompt". A safer unattended version is claude --bare -p "your prompt" --allowedTools "Read,Edit" --max-turns 15 --max-budget-usd 2 --output-format json. Pipe data in with cat file | claude -p "explain".

What is headless mode, in general?

Outside Claude Code, "headless" means software running without its graphical or interactive interface, like headless Chrome for browser automation or a headless server with no monitor. Claude Code uses the word the same way: the agent works, but there's no interface for a person to watch or answer.

What does Claude Code headless plan mode mean?

It means running claude -p "..." --permission-mode plan. In plan mode, "Claude reads files, runs shell commands to explore, and writes a plan, but does not edit your source" (Permission modes). Headless, that gives you a read-only report, such as a refactor proposal written to a log, with no risk of file changes. Shell commands outside the read-only set still need approval, so in -p they're denied unless allowed.

Does Claude Code headless mode use a different model than interactive mode?

No. Headless runs use the same default as interactive sessions, which is Opus 5.5 for Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise and Anthropic API accounts (Model configuration). Override it per run with --model sonnet or --model haiku, and add --fallback-model sonnet,haiku for when the primary model is overloaded.

item.title: Claude Code Subagents Model Selection: Role-by-Role Table
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: Claude Code subagents model selection made practical: when to give each subagent Haiku, Sonnet, Opus or inherit, with official prices, steps and fixes.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

To choose models for Claude Code subagents, set model: in each subagent's frontmatter. Use haiku for high-volume, low-ambiguity jobs like triage, log filtering and file search. Use sonnet for most coding and review agents, and keep opus for the few agents whose mistakes are expensive, like architecture planning or security review. Anthropic's own cost guide says it directly: "For simple subagent tasks, specify model: haiku" (Claude Code costs). The docs show the syntax. This guide adds a way to decide by role, the price math (as of October 2026), and the one precedence rule that can quietly cancel your choice.

Which option is right for you?

If you're new to subagents, put model: sonnet on every custom subagent. Then move single agents down to Haiku or up to Opus once you've seen how they actually perform.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner, writing your first 1–3 subagentsmodel: sonnet on each one. It's Anthropic's stated default for "daily coding tasks" (model config)Create custom subagents
Daily work on a Pro or Max planSonnet for coding agents, Haiku for search and summarize agents, inherit only where you want /model switches to carry overManage costs
Tight budget on API billingHaiku for every read-only or repetitive agent. Opus only for one planning or review agentPricing
Unattended cron or headless pipelinesAn explicit model on every agent (no inherit), plus CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL as a fallbackSub-agents: choose a model
Security-critical or architectural reviewmodel: opus on that one agent, called rarely and on purpose with an @-mentionChoosing a model

Why Sonnet first: in Anthropic's words, "Sonnet handles most coding tasks well and costs less than Opus" (costs). Starting there gives you a baseline you can compare against before you adjust anything.

What is the model field in Claude Code subagents?

The model field is an optional frontmatter key in a Claude Code subagent file. It sets which Claude model runs that subagent, independent of your main session.

Subagents are Markdown files with YAML frontmatter. Put them in .claude/agents/ for one project or ~/.claude/agents/ for every project. Both folders are scanned recursively, so subfolders like agents/review/ work (sub-agents). According to the frontmatter reference, model accepts:

  • An alias: sonnet, opus, haiku, or fable
  • A full model ID such as claude-opus-5-5, the same values the --model flag accepts
  • inherit, which uses the same model as the main conversation
  • Nothing at all. If you leave it out, Claude Code works down its resolution order, which ends at the main conversation's model (sub-agents)

On the Anthropic API, as of October 2026, the aliases resolve to Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5. On Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud, sonnet and haiku still point to Sonnet 4.5 and Haiku 4.5 (model config). If you're on a cloud provider, check that table before you assume you're getting the newest model.

Steps: add a model to a subagent

  1. In your project root, create the folder: mkdir -p .claude/agents.
  2. Create .claude/agents/code-reviewer.md with this frontmatter. It's the example from the official docs:
---
name: code-reviewer
description: Reviews code for quality and best practices
tools: Read, Glob, Grep
model: sonnet
---

You are a code reviewer. When invoked, analyze the code and provide
specific, actionable feedback on quality, security, and best practices.
  1. Optionally add effort: low|medium|high|xhigh|max. It "Overrides the session effort level" for this subagent only (sub-agents).
  2. Call it explicitly by typing @ and choosing it from the typeahead, for example @"code-reviewer (agent)" look at the auth changes.
  3. While it runs, type /tasks. The subagent's row shows the model it's actually using (sub-agents).

Note: from Claude Code v2.1.198, /agents no longer opens the old wizard with Running and Library tabs. It shows a reminder to edit the folders directly or to ask Claude to create the subagent for you (sub-agents). If an older tutorial tells you to click through Library, edit the file instead.

If you're also limiting what each agent can touch, the tools: line goes in the same frontmatter. See Claude Code Subagent allowed-tools: Syntax, Examples, Fixes.

Haiku vs Sonnet vs Opus: which should I use for subagents?

Use Haiku for repetitive, well-defined work, Sonnet for most coding agents, and Opus for complex planning where errors are costly.

Anthropic's own short descriptions line up with these roles. Haiku 5.5 is "For high-volume, latency-sensitive tasks such as classification, extraction, and routing" (models overview). The Choosing a model matrix even lists "sub-agent tasks" as a Haiku use case (choosing a model). The cost guide says to "Reserve Opus for complex architectural decisions or multi-step reasoning" (costs).

Haiku 5.5Sonnet 5.5Opus 5.5Fable 5.1
Alias in frontmatterhaikusonnetopusfable
Input / output price per MTokFrom $0.10 / $0.50$2 / $10$4 / $20$10 / $50
Comparative latencyFastestFastModerateSlower
Default API effortmediumhighmediumhigh
Context window / max output1M / 128K1M / 128K1M / 128K1M / 128K
Good subagent rolesFile search, log triage, test-output summary, labeling, routingImplementing, debugging, everyday code review, doc writingArchitecture plans, security review, large refactor plansHours-long research or agent runs where Opus already fell short
Not forAmbiguous multi-file changesRare, high-stakes decisionsAnything you call dozens of times a dayBudget-capped pipelines

Prices and specs are from the models overview (as of October 2026; check the official page).

Here's a rule of thumb for each role. Ask what one wrong answer from this agent would cost you, and how often the agent runs. Low cost of error and high frequency points to Haiku. High cost of error and low frequency points to Opus. Everything else is Sonnet.

One limitation of this framework: the price gap between Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 is only 2x, so a single Opus agent called a few times a day may cost less than you'd expect. The gap that really matters for recurring work is between Sonnet and Haiku, which is roughly 20x on base prices.

How do I choose a model for a code review subagent?

Default a code review subagent to Sonnet. Drop to Haiku for mechanical checks like style or lint, and switch to Opus for security-sensitive or architectural reviews.

Review means reading a diff alongside the files it touches and judging intent. That's contextual reasoning, so Sonnet is the safe default, and it's what the official code-reviewer example uses. A practical way to split it is two or three review agents instead of one:

Example agentModelToolsWhat it checks
style-checkerhaikuRead, Grep, Bash(npm run lint)Naming, formatting, lint output, missing docstrings
code-reviewersonnetRead, Glob, GrepLogic errors, test coverage, readability
security-revieweropusRead, Glob, GrepAuth, input validation, secrets, permission boundaries

(Example layout, not an official template.)

Pitfalls with review agents

  • A vague description triggers the expensive agent too often. Claude "uses each subagent's description to decide when to delegate tasks" (sub-agents). If your Opus security reviewer's description says "use proactively for any code change," it'll run on every edit. Fix: leave out the word "proactively" for Opus agents and call them with an @-mention instead.
  • Haiku reviewing a refactor. A style agent that's asked "is this refactor safe?" will still answer, and the answer may be shallow. Fix: put the agent's scope in its system prompt, e.g. "Only report lint and formatting issues; say 'out of scope' for logic questions."
  • Too many tokens per review. Lint output and test logs are long. Filtering them with a hook before the agent sees them keeps any model cheaper. The official cost guide shows a PreToolUse hook that greps test output down to failures (costs), and Claude Code Hooks Examples: 7 Copy-Paste Scripts has more patterns like it.

How to reduce cost when running multiple subagents?

Put Haiku on your high-frequency, low-complexity subagents and Sonnet or Opus on the rarely called, reasoning-heavy ones. Cost scales with model price times call volume.

Every subagent "runs in its own context window with its own requests," and those requests count toward the same limits as your main conversation (sub-agents). On a Pro or Max plan, that means usage limits. On API billing, it means dollars.

Example cost math (illustrative numbers, not measurements)

Say a triage subagent reads 50,000 input tokens and writes 5,000 output tokens per run, and a cron job fires it 30 times a day. Using base list prices, with no caching:

ModelCost per run30 runs/day~30 days
Haiku 5.5 ($0.10 / $0.50)$0.0075$0.23~$7
Sonnet 5.5 ($2 / $10)$0.15$4.50~$135
Opus 5.5 ($4 / $20)$0.30$9.00~$270

Prices from the models overview and Haiku 5.5 page (as of October 2026; check the official page). Your real numbers will differ. Prompt caching lowers them, since cache reads cost 10% of base input, or 5% on Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5. Thinking pushes them up, because "Thinking tokens are billed as output tokens" (costs).

Three Haiku pricing details that change the math

  1. Haiku 5.5 has two price tiers. It costs $0.10/$0.50 per MTok "for prompts up to 100,000 tokens" and $0.50/$2.50 above that (Haiku 5.5). A Haiku agent that loads a huge log costs 5x more per token. Keep Haiku prompts under 100K by trimming input with hooks or narrower file globs.
  2. The tokenizer changed. The same text counts as "approximately 30% more tokens than on Claude Haiku 4.5" (Haiku 5.5). Old per-run estimates from Haiku 4.5 will undercount.
  3. You can't switch thinking off. Thinking can't be disabled on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 or Fable (costs). For cheap agents, lower effort instead. Anthropic notes "Tuning effort is often a better lever than switching models" (choosing a model).

The built-in Explore agent

Claude Code ships a built-in Explore subagent for file discovery and code search. With a Claude subscription or Console login, it runs on the model the opus alias resolves to, not your session model (sub-agents). If you want cheaper searches, create your own subagent named Explore with model: haiku. The docs say a user or project subagent with that name overrides the built-in one.

See where the tokens go

Run /usage. On Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise plans it shows usage attributed to "skills, subagents, plugins, and individual MCP servers" as percentages (costs). Start with the subagent that has the biggest share. For a full walkthrough of the numbers, see Claude Code: How to See Token Usage (and Reduce It).

What does the inherit model setting do in subagents?

model: inherit makes a Claude Code subagent run on the main conversation's current model. Config stays simple, but you lose per-agent cost control.

Inherit follows you around. If you type /model opus mid-session, the switch "reaches subagents that inherit the main conversation's model" (model config). That's useful for an implementer agent that should always match your thinking power. It's a cost trap for a summarize-the-logs agent that was fine on Haiku.

There's also a subtle alias rule. If you set model: opus and your main session is already on an Opus model, the subagent uses your session's exact model, including a [1m] suffix and its extended context (sub-agents).

When to use inherit vs. an explicit model

Use inherit whenUse an explicit model when
The agent does the same kind of work as your main session (implementing, debugging)The agent's job is clearly cheaper or harder than your main work
You switch models often and want the agent to followThe agent runs unattended (cron, CI, headless -p)
You only use one or two subagentsYou run several agents in one session

Steps: convert inherit agents safely

  1. List your agents: ls .claude/agents ~/.claude/agents.
  2. Search for agents with no model or with inherit: grep -L "^model:" .claude/agents/.md and grep -l "model: inherit" .claude/agents/.md.
  3. For each one, decide on Haiku, Sonnet or Opus using the table above, and edit the line.
  4. Start a run and confirm the model in /tasks.

A common mistake is assuming that leaving model out means "Sonnet." It doesn't. With no frontmatter model and no CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL, the agent falls through to the main conversation's model (sub-agents). In practice, that's the same as inherit.

Can I use different models for different subagents in the same project?

Yes. Each Claude Code subagent file sets its own model, so one project can run Haiku, Sonnet and Opus agents side by side without them affecting each other.

Example project layout (illustrative)

.claude/agents/
├── research/
│   ├── Explore.md          # model: haiku  (overrides built-in Explore)
│   └── log-triage.md       # model: haiku, effort: low
├── build/
│   ├── implementer.md      # model: inherit
│   └── test-fixer.md       # model: sonnet
└── review/
    ├── code-reviewer.md    # model: sonnet
    └── security-reviewer.md # model: opus

Folder order matters when names clash. Managed settings beat the --agents flag, which beats .claude/agents/, which beats ~/.claude/agents/, which beats plugin agents (sub-agents). A project code-reviewer on Sonnet will override a personal code-reviewer on Opus.

The precedence rule that can override your choice

This is the part most guides skip. "When Claude invokes a subagent, it can also pass a model parameter for that specific invocation," and that parameter comes first in the resolution order, ahead of your frontmatter (sub-agents). The full order:

  1. The per-invocation model parameter (Claude's choice at call time)
  2. The subagent's model frontmatter
  3. The CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL environment variable
  4. The main conversation's model

So model: haiku is a default, not a guarantee. One developer reported on DEV Community that 21 of 25 subagent calls in their logs explicitly asked for Opus despite their Sonnet setup (DEV Community). That's one user's report, not an official figure, but it shows why you should check /tasks.

Your options if it happens:

  • Force one model for everything. Set CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL plus CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE=1 in the env block of your settings (Claude Code v2.1.257+). The limitation: Claude Code then "ignores the model field in subagent definitions," so you lose per-agent mixing (sub-agents).
  • Use a mod. If an installed mod sets a model in its agent.spawn hook, that replaces the per-invocation parameter (sub-agents). This suits people comfortable with plugins, and is probably too much for a first setup.
  • Ask in CLAUDE.md. Add a line like "When starting subagents, do not pass a model parameter; use each agent's configured model." It's a soft instruction, so verify it with /tasks.

Also note that before v2.1.251, CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL beat both frontmatter and per-call parameters (sub-agents). If you're on an older version, upgrade before trusting per-agent settings. Run claude --version to check.

For unattended runs, pair this with Claude Code Cron Job Setup: Run Automations Overnight so the models are fixed before anything runs at 3 a.m.

What are the risks of using Haiku for complex subagent tasks?

The main risk with Haiku on complex subagent work is shallow reasoning. It can miss edge cases in multi-file changes or misread ambiguous instructions, and the result looks confident.

Anthropic positions Haiku 5.5 for "classification, routing, extraction, and subagent tasks" (Haiku 5.5). It puts large-scale refactoring and complex systems engineering under Opus in its selection matrix (choosing a model). Using Haiku outside that range rarely fails loudly. The more likely result is a plausible summary with a missing piece.

Where it tends to go wrong (examples)

  • Multi-file refactors. Changing a function signature requires finding every call site and reasoning about side effects. Keep Haiku read-only here. Let it list call sites and let a Sonnet agent make the edits.
  • Ambiguous prompts. "Clean up the auth module" has many valid readings. A cheaper model may pick one without saying so. Write success criteria into the agent's prompt.
  • Silent scope creep. A Haiku agent with Write and Edit tools can make changes you didn't expect. Give Haiku agents read-only tools (Read, Glob, Grep) unless the task is truly mechanical.
  • Verbose context. Above 100K prompt tokens, Haiku's price rises 5x (Haiku 5.5), so a big context removes much of the cost advantage too.

How to test before trusting it

Anthropic suggests an "efficiency-first" path: begin with Haiku 5.5, test thoroughly, and "Upgrade only if necessary for specific capability gaps" (choosing a model). For a solo builder, that can be small:

  1. Pick 5–10 past tasks for this agent where you already know the right answer.
  2. Run them with model: haiku, then with model: sonnet.
  3. Compare misses. If Haiku misses things that matter, upgrade that one agent and leave the others alone.

Add guardrails so a weaker agent can't do damage. AI Agent Guardrails Example: Copy-Paste Claude Code Rules has rules you can paste in.

How does subagent model choice affect latency and token limits?

Haiku is the fastest Claude model and Fable the slowest. All four current models share the same 1M-token context and 128K-token output limits, so the choice mostly affects speed and price, not capacity.

Spec (as of October 2026)Haiku 5.5Sonnet 5.5Opus 5.5Fable 5.1
Comparative latencyFastestFastModerateSlower
Context window1M1M1M1M
Max output (sync API)128K128K128K128K
Effort levels in Claude Codelow → maxlow → maxlow → maxlow → max

Sources: models overview, model config. The overview adds that "Actual latency depends on prompt length, output length, and thinking effort." Lower effort can make a slow model feel faster, and max can make Haiku slow.

Subagents also add latency of their own. Non-fork subagents "start fresh and may need time to gather context," so delegation is slower than doing the work in the main conversation (sub-agents). For an agent in a tight loop, such as one called once per file across 200 files, both effects add up. Haiku with effort: low is the natural pick there, provided the task is mechanical.

Rate limits are the other limit to watch. Parallel subagents send requests at the same time. On API billing, Anthropic's suggested per-user rate for 1–5 user teams is 200k–300k tokens per minute and 5–7 requests per minute (costs). Several Opus agents running in parallel will hit that sooner. If your overnight jobs stop with a limit error, see Claude Code Rate Limit Reached: Retry Setup for Cron Jobs.

Next steps

Do it yourself today:

  1. Run grep -L "^model:" .claude/agents/.md ~/.claude/agents/.md and give every listed agent an explicit model, using the role table above.
  2. Create .claude/agents/Explore.md with model: haiku and read-only tools if you're on a subscription and search-heavy work is eating your limits.
  3. Run your usual workflow once, then open /usage and /tasks to confirm each agent ran on the model you set.

If you'd rather not manage this yourself: the main official lever is your plan. Claude Pro is $20/month and Max starts at $100/month, and both include Claude Code (as of October 2026; check claude.com/pricing). A higher plan suits people who'd rather buy more headroom than tune agent configs. It's a poor fit if you're mainly trying to cut costs, because usage still adds up. For Team or Enterprise seats, admins get spend reports and limits in the admin console (costs). That helps small teams, but it's more than a solo builder needs.

Related guides on this site:

  • Claude Code Subagent allowed-tools: Syntax, Examples, Fixes
  • Claude Code: How to See Token Usage (and Reduce It)
  • Claude Code Permissions Best Practices: Headless Template
  • Why Claude Code Stops Mid-Automation (and How to Fix It)

FAQ

What is the model field in Claude Code subagents?

It's an optional frontmatter key in a subagent's Markdown file that picks the model for that agent. It accepts haiku, sonnet, opus, fable, a full model ID such as claude-opus-5-5, or inherit (sub-agents). If you leave it out, the agent usually ends up on your main conversation's model.

Can I use different models for different subagents in the same project?

Yes. Each file in .claude/agents/ declares its own model, so Haiku, Sonnet and Opus agents can sit side by side. Keep in mind that Claude can pass a per-call model parameter that overrides frontmatter, so check /tasks to see what actually ran.

What does the inherit model setting do in subagents?

It makes the subagent use whatever model your main session is on, and a /model switch carries over to it (model config). Use it for agents that do the same work as you. Avoid it for cheap, repetitive agents and unattended jobs.

What are the risks of using Haiku for complex subagent tasks?

Haiku is built for high-volume work like classification, routing and extraction. On multi-file refactors or vague instructions it can return confident but incomplete results. Keep Haiku agents read-only and narrowly scoped, and test them on known past tasks before relying on them.

Does the main conversation's model matter if every subagent has its own model?

Yes, a little. The main conversation still pays for its own tokens and orchestration, and the built-in Plan subagent inherits it (sub-agents). Anthropic's cost guide links unexpectedly high spend to "Opus left as the default model" (costs).
