item.title: Claude Code Stuck on Compacting Conversation: Cron Watchdog
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: Claude Code stuck on compacting conversation? Why it hangs in headless and cron runs, the real auto-compact defaults, and a watchdog script that recovers.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

If Claude Code is stuck on "Compacting conversation," stop the process. Then start a fresh session with a short written handoff instead of waiting or resuming. In an unattended claude -p run, wrap the command in a wall-clock timeout and use the PreCompact/PostCompact hooks to timestamp each compaction. If one runs too long, kill the run and retry clean. The rest of this guide covers why compaction stalls, what the real thresholds are, and how to make a cron job recover without you.

The official docs warn that /compact "reads the conversation it summarizes, so compacting a large context is itself a large request" (Claude Code docs: Manage costs). A large request can fail, get retried or run slowly, and in a headless run nobody sees the spinner.

Which option is right for you?

Pick based on how you run Claude Code today. Each row gives the first page to open.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner, interactive terminal, spinner frozen right nowPress Esc, then /compact with a focus, or /clearErrors: Prompt is too long
Daily work: cron or CI job that sometimes never finishesWrapper script with a hard timeout and a compaction watchdog (below)Run Claude Code programmatically
Long multi-hour agent tasksCompact earlier with CLAUDE_AUTOCOMPACT_PCT_OVERRIDE=50, and split work into sessionsSet the auto-compact window
Budget-sensitive (API key billing)Cap each run with --max-budget-usd and --max-turns, and turn auto-compact off for short jobsCLI reference
Not sure if it's compaction at allCheck the stream for api_retry events before blaming compaction/why-claude-code-stops-mid-automation-and-how-to-fix-it/

Here's why each one fits. Interactive users can see and answer the error. Cron users can't, so they need a script that decides for them. Long tasks gain the most from compacting at a smaller, cheaper context. Budget users mainly need a ceiling so a stuck loop can't run up a bill.

Why does Claude Code get stuck on "Compacting conversation"?

Claude Code gets stuck when the summarization request fails, retries or loops. Most often the context is too big to summarize, or the API is slow or throttled.

The documented and reported causes fall into five groups:

  1. The summary doesn't fit. The errors page lists Prompt is too long · automatic compaction failed: Compaction would make the conversation longer. That message means the summary would be bigger than the original, and the fix is /clear (Errors reference). The same page says a single-exchange conversation "cannot be compacted" at all.
  2. Retries that look like a hang. Claude Code "retries transient failures up to 10 times with exponential backoff before showing you an error." Each attempt gets up to API_TIMEOUT_MS (600000 ms, 10 minutes by default) to receive response headers (Errors: Automatic retries; Environment variables). A big compaction request that hits an overloaded API can therefore sit for a long time before it fails.
  3. The retry watchdog you turned on. Setting CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG=1 makes Claude Code retry 429 and 529 errors indefinitely. On v2.1.199 and later it also raises the retry count for other transient errors to 300, "roughly three hours of backoff" (Errors: Tune retry behavior). That's useful for cron. It also means a compaction can wait hours unless you set CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG_MAX_WAIT_MS.
  4. Thrashing loops. GitHub issue #6004 describes an endless cycle: read files, compact, lose the state, then read the same files again. It was reported on v1.0.83, still seen on v2.0.6x, and closed as "not planned" in February 2026. The usual trigger is one large file or tool output that fills the context again right after each summary.
  5. Summarizer overflow (older versions). Issue #23751 reported Conversation too long failures at about 48% context usage on v2.1.32–v2.1.34, with image-heavy sessions hit hardest. It is marked fixed as of v2.1.85. If your cron box runs an old pinned version, update it first.

Here's why headless makes this worse. An interactive user sees the error and presses Esc. A claude -p process has no human, so a failed compaction ends in one of two ways. It either exits non-zero, which is easy to handle, or it keeps retrying or looping, which looks like a frozen job.

Example: a nightly job that reads a 10,000-line log file can fill most of the context in one tool call. Compaction summarizes it, the agent reads the log again, and the cycle repeats until the job hits a limit or you notice in the morning.

What triggers auto-compact, and can you change the threshold?

By default, Claude Code auto-compacts when the conversation reaches the model's context limit. You can lower that point with a setting, a CLI flag or an environment variable.

The "92–95%" figure you see quoted online doesn't match current docs. According to Default auto-compact thresholds (as of October 2026):

  • Most sessions compact when the conversation reaches the model's context limit.
  • Models with a native 1M window (Fable models, Sonnet 5 and later, Haiku 5.5, Opus 4.7 and later) compact "at about 967K tokens by default."
  • Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.6 without extended context compact at the 200K boundary.
  • With CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_1M_CONTEXT=1, native-1M models compact at 200K.
  • Unrecognized model IDs, such as an LLM gateway alias, compact at whatever window Claude Code assumes for that ID.

The four ways to change it

WhereHowScope
In a session/autocompact 500k (or /autocompact auto to reset)Saved for the current model
Settings file"autoCompactWindow": 200000 in ~/.claude/settings.jsonEvery model
One launchclaude --autocompact 500k (v2.1.221+)That run only
Scripts/CICLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW=200000Wins over the others

Accepted values run from 100K to 1M tokens, and Claude Code caps the window at the model's context size (model config; settings reference).

Use CLAUDE_AUTOCOMPACT_PCT_OVERRIDE to compact earlier as a percentage. The docs say "the variable can't raise the threshold, so values above the default percentage are ignored" (Environment variables). It only applies in sessions that compact before the model's context limit. So pair it with CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW if you want it to take effect.

Turning it off

Set "autoCompactEnabled": false in a settings file (settings reference). With auto-compact off, a full context produces a Context limit reached error instead of a compaction (Errors). For a short cron job that's often what you want: a fast, loud failure your script can catch. For long jobs, it means the run just stops at the limit.

There's also a hook-level off switch. A PreCompact hook that exits with code 2 blocks compaction (Hooks reference). See /claude-code-hooks-lifecycle-every-event-explained/ for where it fires in the lifecycle.

How do you detect a stuck compaction in a headless or cron run?

To spot a stuck compaction in headless Claude Code, mark when each compaction starts and ends. If a start has no matching end within your limit, the run is stuck.

Exit codes alone aren't enough. The docs say Claude Code "exits with code 0 on success and a non-zero code when the run fails" (Headless docs). A hung process never exits, though, so you also need signals that work while it's still running. There are three:

  1. Compaction markers from hooks. PreCompact fires "before context compaction begins" and PostCompact fires "after context compaction completes successfully." Both accept an auto or manual matcher (Hooks reference). Have the first write a timestamp file and the second delete it. A timestamp file older than your limit means compaction is stuck.
  2. Stream inactivity. Run with --output-format stream-json --verbose and write stdout to a file. If the file hasn't changed in N minutes, something is wrong. Note that PreCompact and PostCompact "never produce a hook_started event" in the stream (CLI reference), so the hook marker files are the more reliable signal.
  3. Retry events. Before each retry, the stream includes a system/api_retry event with attempt, max_retries, retry_delay_ms and an error category such as rate_limit or overloaded (Headless docs). Several of these right after the marker file appears means compaction is fighting the API rather than looping.

Steps to add compaction markers

  1. Create a job folder, for example mkdir -p ~/jobs/nightly/state.
  2. Save this as ~/jobs/nightly/compact-watch.json. It's an example; change the paths to match yours:
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreCompact": [
      { "matcher": "auto",
        "hooks": [{ "type": "command",
          "command": "date +%s > \"$HOME/jobs/nightly/state/compact.started\"" }] }
    ],
    "PostCompact": [
      { "matcher": "auto",
        "hooks": [{ "type": "command",
          "command": "rm -f \"$HOME/jobs/nightly/state/compact.started\"; date >> \"$HOME/jobs/nightly/state/compact.log\"" }] }
    ]
  }
}
  1. Pass it with --settings ./compact-watch.json. In --bare mode Claude Code skips hooks it would normally discover on disk. Settings you pass with --settings are still loaded (Headless: bare mode).
  2. Watch the state/ folder from your wrapper script (next section).

A common mistake is putting the hooks only in .claude/settings.json and then running with --bare. The hooks silently never fire. The fix is to pass them through --settings.

How do you set a timeout and kill a hung Claude Code process?

Claude Code has no built-in wall-clock limit for claude -p. Wrap it in timeout or a watchdog loop, send SIGTERM first, then SIGKILL after a grace period.

What the docs give you for runaway work: --max-turns "exits with an error when the limit is reached" and has no limit by default. --max-budget-usd stops the run once estimated spend reaches the cap (CLI reference). Neither one measures time. A single compaction that keeps retrying uses no extra turns, so you need a clock as well.

Option A: GNU timeout (Linux)

timeout -k 30s 90m claude -p "$(cat task.md)" --output-format json --max-turns 40
echo "exit=$?"

GNU timeout sends TERM when the limit is reached and KILL 30 seconds later because of -k. It exits with status 124 when the command timed out (GNU coreutils: timeout invocation).

Here's what happens inside Claude Code on SIGTERM: "Claude Code exits with code 143," leaves the current turn unfinished, kills any running Bash process tree and runs SessionEnd hooks (Headless: Stop a run with SIGTERM). If you'd rather end the turn cleanly, the docs say to send SIGINT first.

Option B: watchdog loop (works anywhere, catches compaction specifically)

This example script combines a total time limit, a compaction limit and a stream-inactivity check. The limits are example values; tune them to your job.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# run-agent.sh — example watchdog for one unattended Claude Code run
set -u
JOB="$HOME/jobs/nightly"; STATE="$JOB/state"
COMPACT_LIMIT=900     # example: 15 min max for one compaction
HARD_LIMIT=5400       # example: 90 min for the whole run
IDLE_MIN=20           # example: no stream output for 20 min = stalled
mkdir -p "$STATE"; rm -f "$STATE/compact.started"

cd "$JOB/repo" || exit 1
claude -p "$(cat "$JOB/task.md")" \
  --settings "$JOB/compact-watch.json" \
  --output-format stream-json --verbose \
  --max-turns 40 --permission-prompts none \
  > "$STATE/stream.jsonl" 2> "$STATE/stderr.log" &
PID=$!; START=$(date +%s)

stop() { echo "$(date) $1" >> "$STATE/watchdog.log"
         kill -INT "$PID" 2>/dev/null; sleep 10
         kill -TERM "$PID" 2>/dev/null; sleep 20
         kill -KILL "$PID" 2>/dev/null; exit "$2"; }

while kill -0 "$PID" 2>/dev/null; do
  sleep 30; NOW=$(date +%s)
  if [ -f "$STATE/compact.started" ] && \
     [ $((NOW - $(cat "$STATE/compact.started"))) -gt "$COMPACT_LIMIT" ]; then
    stop "compaction stalled" 75
  fi
  [ $((NOW - START)) -gt "$HARD_LIMIT" ] && stop "hard limit" 124
  [ -n "$(find "$STATE/stream.jsonl" -mmin +"$IDLE_MIN")" ] && stop "stream idle" 76
done
wait "$PID"; exit $?

The exit codes 75 and 76 are this script's own convention, so your retry layer can tell a stalled compaction apart from a normal failure. --permission-prompts none (v2.1.259+) stops the run from waiting on a permission prompt nobody will answer (Headless docs). That's a separate kind of hang that looks the same from outside.

Pitfalls

  • Killing too early. A normal compaction of a large context takes real time, and each API attempt can wait up to 10 minutes for headers by default. A 2-minute limit will kill healthy runs. Start around 15 minutes and look at compact.log to see how long yours actually take.
  • Mistaking background wait for a hang. After the final turn, claude -p can wait up to 10 minutes for background subagents or commands (CLAUDE_CODE_PRINT_BG_WAIT_CEILING_MS, default 600000) (Environment variables). If stderr shows Waiting for background work to finish, it isn't compaction.
  • Killing only the parent. If you launch through bash -c or npx, signal the process group. Otherwise a child claude can keep running.

How do you avoid hitting compaction at all?

Keep each Claude Code session well below the auto-compact window. Filter big tool outputs, send verbose work to subagents, and give each task its own session.

These are the levers that matter most for unattended jobs, roughly in order of payoff:

  1. One job, one session. Start every cron run fresh (no --continue). The docs recommend /clear "when switching to unrelated work," and a new -p process does the same thing (Context window docs).
  2. Filter output before Claude sees it. The docs' own example is a PreToolUse hook that rewrites test commands to keep only failures. They point out that grepping a 10,000-line log for ERROR can cut context "from tens of thousands of tokens to hundreds" (Manage costs). Copy-paste versions are in /claude-code-hooks-examples-7-copy-paste-scripts/.
  3. Delegate large reads to subagents. Their file contents stay in their own context window, and only a summary comes back (Context window docs).
  4. Use --bare for scripts. The docs say "--bare is the recommended mode for scripted and SDK calls" (Headless docs). It skips CLAUDE.md, MCP servers, skills and auto memory, so the run starts with less context. Bare mode needs ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, because it doesn't use your subscription login.
  5. Trim always-loaded files. Keep CLAUDE.md under 200 lines and move workflow-specific instructions into skills, which load only when invoked (Manage costs).
  6. Compact earlier if you must compact. A summary of a 150K context is a smaller request than a summary of 950K. On a native-1M model, example settings like CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW=300000 keep each compaction request moderate.

To measure what's filling the context, run /context in an interactive session on the same repo. It "shows your conversation size in tokens" broken down by category (Errors). /claude-code-how-to-see-token-usage-and-reduce-it/ walks through reading that output.

A common mistake is asking an agent to "read all files in src/ and summarize". That's the quickest way to fill the window. Name the files instead, or have a subagent do the reading.

How do you resume a session safely after a compaction failure?

After a failed compaction, don't resume the stuck Claude Code session. Start a new session seeded with a short handoff file, and keep the old transcript for debugging.

Here's why. --resume and --continue reload the stored conversation. That's the same oversized history that just failed to compact, so the next turn is likely to trigger the same compaction. Two details make this worse after a kill:

  • After SIGTERM, "Claude Code leaves the interrupted turn as it is, and your next prompt drives the conversation." Setting CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_INTERRUPTED_TURN=1 makes it continue the interrupted turn instead (Headless docs). That's the opposite of what you want here.
  • If you resume with different system-prompt flags, they only take effect "once the conversation is compacted or when you start a new conversation" (CLI reference).

Safer recovery steps

  1. Record the failed session ID. With --output-format stream-json, the system/init event and the final result carry session_id. Save it to state/last_session from your wrapper.
  2. Keep a progress file the agent writes. Add this line to task.md (example wording): "After each completed step, append one line to PROGRESS.md: step, files changed, what's next."
  3. Start fresh with a handoff. Example: claude -p "Continue the task in task.md. Completed steps are in PROGRESS.md; verify the last one, then continue." --settings compact-watch.json
  4. Only resume if you need the history. Fork it so the original stays intact: claude --resume "$ID" --fork-session (CLI reference). Then run /compact with a narrow focus, for example /compact keep only the list of changed files and the failing test name.
  5. Check the code state. A killed run may have left half-written files. git status and git stash handle most cases. /claude-code-checkpoints-how-rollback-works-in-automations/ explains what Claude Code's own checkpoints do and don't cover.

In an interactive terminal, the errors page and community reports give a shorter path. Press Esc twice to step back a few messages, then run /compact again. If that still has no room, use /clear; the old conversation stays reachable through /resume (Errors).

How do you build auto-recovery for unattended runs (cron, CI)?

A watchdog kills the stalled Claude Code run, and a wrapper retries it once in a fresh session. The wrapper also sorts exit codes and logs anything it can't fix.

Building on the watchdog script above, a minimal recovery layer looks like this (example):

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# nightly.sh — called from cron
JOB="$HOME/jobs/nightly"
for attempt in 1 2; do
  "$JOB/run-agent.sh"; code=$?
  case $code in
    0)  echo "$(date) ok attempt=$attempt" >> "$JOB/state/history.log"; exit 0 ;;
    75|76|124|143)  # stalled compaction, idle stream, hard limit, SIGTERM
        echo "$(date) stalled code=$code attempt=$attempt" >> "$JOB/state/history.log"
        mv "$JOB/state/stream.jsonl" "$JOB/state/stream.$(date +%s).jsonl" ;;
    *)  echo "$(date) failed code=$code" >> "$JOB/state/history.log"; break ;;
  esac
done
exit 1

And the crontab line, for example: 15 2 * /home/you/jobs/nightly/nightly.sh >> /home/you/jobs/nightly/state/cron.log 2>&1. Environment details, such as PATH and auth tokens under cron, are covered in /claude-code-cron-job-setup-run-automations-overnight/.

Design decisions that matter

  • Retry once, not forever. If the second fresh session also stalls at compaction, the task itself is too big for one session. Retrying again just burns tokens. Issue #6004 includes one user's report of $800 in API charges from a compaction loop (GitHub #6004).
  • Bound the API retry wait. If you use CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG=1 to ride out rate limits, also set CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG_MAX_WAIT_MS (v2.1.295+). Otherwise a single compaction request can wait out 429/529 errors without limit (Errors). Rate-limit handling for cron is covered in /claude-code-rate-limit-reached-retry-setup-for-cron-jobs/.
  • Cap money as well as time. Add --max-budget-usd (print mode only). The docs warn spend "can pass the cap, so leave headroom" (CLI reference).
  • Alerting is up to you. Claude Code doesn't page anyone. Have the wrapper's failure branch call whatever you already use: a Slack incoming webhook via curl, mail, or your CI's failure notification.
  • Lower retries if you want fast failure. CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_RETRIES defaults to 10. The docs suggest you "lower it to surface failures faster in scripts" (Errors).

A common mistake is letting the retry layer use --continue. The retry then inherits the same bloated context and stalls the same way. Always retry with a new session plus the progress file.

Claude Code auto-compact vs manual context management: which is more reliable for long runs?

For unattended long runs, manual context management in Claude Code is more predictable. Auto-compact is convenient, but it adds a failure point your script can't control.

ApproachHow you set itStrengthLimitationBest for
Default auto-compactNothingZero setup, the run continues past the limitCompaction happens at the largest, most expensive context, so it's more exposed to slow or failed requestsInteractive work
Earlier auto-compactCLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW, CLAUDE_AUTOCOMPACT_PCT_OVERRIDESmaller summary requestsCompacts more often; each summary can drop detailMulti-hour single tasks
Auto-compact off + chunked sessions"autoCompactEnabled": false, one task per -p run, PROGRESS.md handoffDeterministic: a full context becomes a clean errorYou design the task split up front; a run can stop at the limitCron jobs with clear steps
Subagent isolationDelegate reads/tests to subagentsMain context stays smallSubagents have their own windows and can compact too (sub-agents docs)Research-heavy jobs
Block via hookPreCompact exits 2Fine-grained control, e.g. block only during a critical stepBlocking leaves you at the limit with no reliefRare, advanced cases

My pick for the reader of this guide: for recurring jobs, use chunked sessions with auto-compact either off or set to a lower window, plus the watchdog. Here's why. A job that fails loudly at step 3 of 5 is easy to resume from PROGRESS.md. A job that freezes in a summary at 2 a.m. costs you a night.

One pitfall with turning compaction off: if a single step needs more context than the window holds, it will always fail. Split that step further, or move its large reads into a subagent. /ai-agent-vs-automation-a-5-question-test-for-claude-code/ helps decide whether a step needs an agent at all.

Next steps

Do today (DIY):

  1. Run claude --version on the machine that runs your cron. If it's older than v2.1.85, update with claude update. The summarizer overflow bug in issue #23751 was fixed in that version.
  2. Add compact-watch.json and run-agent.sh from this guide to one job, with generous limits (15 min per compaction, 90 min total). Run it for a week and read compact.log to see real compaction durations.
  3. Add a "write one line to PROGRESS.md per step" instruction to your task prompt, so any kill can be retried in a fresh session.

If you'd rather not do it yourself: Anthropic's official Claude Code GitHub Actions integration runs Claude Code inside a CI job. The CI runner gives you job timeouts and failure notifications, so you don't maintain a cron box. It suits people already on GitHub. It doesn't suit jobs that need your local machine or private network, and you still pay for Actions minutes plus Claude usage.

If your real problem is hitting usage limits rather than hangs, Claude subscriptions include Claude Code. Pro is "$20 if billed monthly" and Max starts "from $100 per month" (as of October 2026; check the official pricing page). A bigger plan doesn't fix a stuck compaction, though. It only gives you more headroom before rate limits slow the retries.

FAQ

Why is Claude Code frozen on compacting conversation?

Usually the summary request is very large and is either retrying against a slow or throttled API, or caught in a re-read-and-compact loop. Each attempt can wait up to 10 minutes for response headers by default, and Claude Code retries up to 10 times (Errors). In a terminal, press Esc and run /compact with a focus, or /clear.

How do I force Claude Code to stop compacting?

Interactively, press Esc to interrupt, then /clear for a fresh context. In scripts, send SIGINT or SIGTERM to the process; SIGTERM exits with code 143 (Headless docs). To prevent it, a PreCompact hook that exits with code 2 blocks compaction.

Does Claude Code auto-compact affect cron jobs?

Yes. claude -p runs use the same auto-compact thresholds as interactive sessions, but nobody sees the spinner. A stalled compaction holds the job until something kills it. Add a wall-clock timeout and hook-based compaction markers so the job fails and retries on its own.

Can I disable auto-compact in Claude Code?

Yes. Set "autoCompactEnabled": false in a settings file (settings reference). After that, a full context ends with a Context limit reached error instead of compacting. That suits short, chunked cron jobs better than long single tasks.

What exit code does Claude Code return on timeout?

Claude Code has no built-in time limit for -p, so the code depends on what stopped it. GNU timeout returns 124, SIGTERM gives 143, and --max-turns exits with an error status when the turn limit is hit (GNU timeout; Headless docs; CLI reference).

item.title: Claude Code Subagent allowed-tools: Syntax, Examples, Fixes
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: Claude Code subagent allowed-tools explained: the real field is tools, plus disallowedTools, MCP wildcards, inherit vs restrict, and hooks that enforce it.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

Claude Code subagents don't have an allowed-tools field. The key you want in a subagent's .md frontmatter is tools. It's an allowlist, written as a comma-separated string like tools: Read, Grep, Glob or as a YAML list. disallowedTools is the matching denylist. allowed-tools belongs to Skills, and it does something else: it pre-approves tools for one turn and restricts nothing. If you leave tools out, the subagent "Inherits every tool available to subagents if omitted."

Which option is right for you?

The best place to start depends on whether you want a safe default fast, a dependable daily setup, or the lowest token cost.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner, first custom subagenttools: Read, Grep, Glob (read-only). Nothing can breakCreate custom subagents
Daily work, subagent edits code and runs teststools: Read, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob plus a permissions.deny rule for risky Bash commandsConfigure permissions
Subagent needs one MCP server (GitHub, Slack)tools: Read, mcp__github__*, or scope the server with mcpServersSub-agents: MCP section
You want everything except writesdisallowedTools: Write, Edit and keep inheritingSub-agents: restrict tools
Budget: keep context and tokens smallInline MCP servers in the subagent so the parent never loads their tool descriptionsSub-agents: scope MCP servers
Unattended or cron runsExplicit tools list plus a PreToolUse hook as a second checkHooks reference

The reason for each row: an explicit read-only list can't fail in a dangerous way. A Bash deny rule blocks particular commands without taking Bash away. A server wildcard keeps the list short. A denylist is the least work when you only fear one or two tools. Inline MCP keeps tool definitions out of the main context. Hooks still run when a frontmatter list turns out wrong.

What is the allowed-tools field in Claude Code subagents?

In Claude Code subagents, the "allowed-tools" job is done by the tools frontmatter key, an allowlist that limits which tools that subagent can call. Many people search for allowed-tools because they've seen it in Skills or the Agent SDK, so the three names are worth separating before you write any YAML.

Where you write itKey nameWhat it does
Subagent file (.claude/agents/*.md)toolsAllowlist: the subagent can use only these tools
Subagent filedisallowedToolsDenylist: removes tools from the inherited or listed pool
Skill file (SKILL.md)allowed-toolsPre-approves listed tools for the turn that invokes the skill. Other tools stay callable
Agent SDK optionsallowedTools / allowed_toolsAuto-approves tools before your permission callback runs

The Skills documentation says the Skills allowed-tools grant clears when you send your next message, and that it does not restrict which tools are available. The Agent SDK permissions page treats allowedTools as approval too. Put allowed-tools: in a subagent file and you get neither behavior: it isn't a supported subagent field, so the subagent inherits everything.

Here is a minimal, valid subagent. Save it as .claude/agents/code-reviewer.md (example):

---
name: code-reviewer
description: Reviews diffs for bugs and style issues. Use after code changes.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob
model: sonnet
---
You are a code reviewer. Read the changed files, report problems with file and line, and never modify files.

Some official limits are worth knowing (as of October 2026, sub-agents docs). name can be up to 256 characters and can't contain :. Claude Code warns at startup when the combined descriptions of your custom subagents go over 15,000 tokens. By default, 20 subagents running at once is the ceiling, and the next spawn fails with Concurrent subagent limit reached.

How do you write the allowed-tools syntax (wildcards, lists, MCP tool names)?

Claude Code's subagent tools field takes exact tool names, either as a comma-separated string or a YAML list. The documented wildcards are for MCP servers, such as mcp__github__*.

Steps to add or change a tool list

  1. Open (or create) the file: .claude/agents/<name>.md for one project, or ~/.claude/agents/<name>.md for all your projects. A subagent with the same name in the project folder wins over the one in your home folder. The priority table puts managed settings first, then the --agents CLI flag, then project, then user, then plugins.
  2. Add a tools: line between the --- markers. Spell tool names with their exact capitalization (Read, not read).
  3. Save the file, then start a new session or ask Claude to use the subagent by name.
  4. On current versions, typing /agents only reminds you to ask Claude or edit .claude/agents/ and ~/.claude/agents/ directly. The interactive wizard with Running and Library tabs exists only on v2.1.197 and earlier (sub-agents docs).

Syntax patterns from the official docs

String form:

tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash

YAML list form (same meaning):

tools:
  - Read
  - Grep
  - Glob
  - Bash

Every tool from one MCP server, plus Read:

tools: Read, mcp__github__*

Everything inherited except one MCP server:

disallowedTools: mcp__github

No MCP tools at all, built-ins kept:

disallowedTools: mcp__*

Those three MCP patterns come straight from the sub-agents table. One MCP tool is named mcp__<server>__<tool>, the same format hook matchers use, for example mcp__memory__create_entities.

What the docs don't promise

  • Command-level patterns in tools. Skills accept Bash(git add ). For subagents, the docs only describe what a specifier does in disallowedTools: "An entry with a specifier, such as Bash(git push ), still removes the whole tool." To keep Bash and block only git push, add Bash(git push *) to permissions.deny in settings. That rule covers the main conversation and subagents.
  • Agent(worker, researcher). This allowlist of spawnable subagent types works only for an agent running as the main thread through claude --agent. Inside an ordinary subagent definition, the docs say the type list in parentheses is ignored.
  • Task vs Agent. In v2.1.63 the subagent-spawning tool was renamed from Task to Agent, and older Task(...) references still work as aliases (GitHub issue #29677). Hook scripts that check tool_name == "Task" stopped matching, so use Agent in anything new.

Defining the list from the CLI

For one-off or scripted runs, the --agents flag takes JSON, with tools as an array (sub-agents docs):

claude --agents '{
  "code-reviewer": {
    "description": "Expert code reviewer. Use proactively after code changes.",
    "prompt": "You are a senior code reviewer.",
    "tools": ["Read", "Grep", "Glob", "Bash"],
    "model": "sonnet"
  }
}'

In non-interactive mode you can pass a file path instead, such as claude -p --agents ./agents.json "Review my changes". Interactive sessions refuse a file path (sub-agents docs).

Inherit vs restrict: should a subagent inherit all tools or list them explicitly?

For a Claude Code subagent that runs without you watching, list its tools explicitly. Inheriting is fine for interactive helpers you supervise. If you leave tools out, the subagent picks up every built-in and MCP tool the main conversation has, after a couple of filters. Listing tools gives you predictable behavior, and in exchange you have to update the list when the job changes.

Omit tools (inherit)tools allowlistdisallowedTools denylist
New MCP servers you add laterPicked up automaticallyNot available until you add themPicked up automatically
Risk of surprise side effectsHighestLowestMedium
MaintenanceNoneUpdate when the job changesUpdate when a new risky tool appears
Good forAd-hoc helpers in an interactive sessionCron jobs, reviewers, anything unattended"Everything but writes" style agents
Failure modeDoes too muchMissing tool, or launch refused if nothing resolvesForgetting a new dangerous tool

When both fields are set: "If both are set, disallowedTools is applied first, then tools is resolved against the remaining pool." A tool that appears in both lists ends up removed.

Two inheritance details tend to catch people:

  • Permission mode can be overridden. When the main conversation runs in bypassPermissions, acceptEdits, or auto mode, the subagent runs in that same mode and the docs say your permissionMode setting is ignored. The tool list is your real limit in those modes, so a tight list matters more than the permission mode you picked. To see how modes and rules combine for headless runs, read /claude-code-permissions-best-practices-headless-template/.
  • Built-in agents already restrict. The built-in Explore and Plan agents use "read-only tools; Write and Edit are denied," and general-purpose gets every tool available to subagents (sub-agents docs). If one of those already fits the job, you don't need a custom file.

A practical rule: if the subagent can run when you're not at the keyboard, such as from cron, CI, or a background session, write out its tools. If you start it yourself and watch the output, inheriting is acceptable.

Which tools can be assigned to a Claude Code subagent?

A Claude Code subagent can use any built-in or connected MCP tool, except a few that are always withheld. Built-in names come from the tools reference, which says they "are the exact strings you use in permission rules, subagent tool lists, and hook matchers."

Tools a background subagent keeps

Subagents run in the background by default. A background subagent keeps every MCP tool but only these built-in tools (as of October 2026, sub-agents docs):

GroupTool names
Read and searchRead, Grep, Glob, LSP
Change filesEdit, Write, NotebookEdit
Run commandsBash, PowerShell, Monitor, TaskStop
WebWebFetch, WebSearch
WorkflowTodoWrite, Skill, ToolSearch, SendMessage, Artifact
WorktreesEnterWorktree, ExitWorktree

The list also includes SubagentHandback for a subagent that reports through it, and Agent, which follows the depth limit. Before v2.1.280, background subagents couldn't use LSP (sub-agents docs).

Tools no subagent gets, even if listed

AskUserQuestion, EndConversation, EnterPlanMode, ScheduleWakeup, WaitForMcpServers, Workflow, ExitPlanMode (unless permissionMode is plan), and Agent once the subagent hits the depth limit. Subagents can spawn their own subagents "up to three layers below the main conversation" by default. You change that limit with CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH.

That affects how you design the job. A subagent can't stop and ask you a question, so its prompt has to contain everything it needs. And because the background filter drops some tools silently, "the same definition can resolve to different tools in the foreground and the background."

Starter lists by job (examples)

  • Read-only auditor: Read, Grep, Glob
  • Bug fixer that runs tests: Read, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob
  • Docs writer with citations: Read, Write, WebFetch, WebSearch
  • Issue triager: Read, mcp__github__*

What happens when a subagent's tools don't match its job (failure modes)?

When a Claude Code subagent lacks a tool it needs, it either can't launch or does a weaker version of the task. When it has more tools than it needs, it can change things you never asked it to touch. Here are the failures you're most likely to hit, with fixes.

1. Every entry is wrong, so the subagent won't start

If nothing in tools resolves to a real tool, because of typos, lowercase names, or tools subagents can't have, Claude Code "usually refuses to launch the subagent," and the Agent tool returns an error naming the entries it couldn't resolve (sub-agents docs; errors page). The error text contains "spawned with zero tools." Fix: check capitalization against the tools reference, and remove anything from the withheld list above.

2. Some entries are wrong, and nothing tells you

The error only appears when the list resolves to nothing. Suppose you write tools: Read, edit, Bash (example). edit doesn't resolve, so the subagent starts with Read and Bash. It may then try to make changes through shell commands, or report that it couldn't edit. Fix: after any edit to the list, ask the subagent to name the tools it has before the first real run.

3. Background runs lose a tool you listed

A tool that isn't on the background keep-list gets removed with no error. A definition that works when you watch it in the foreground can then break overnight. Fix: build your lists only from the background table above, or set background: false for interactive use. When a cron run stops halfway, also read /why-claude-code-stops-mid-automation-and-how-to-fix-it/.

4. allowed-tools in a subagent file

That key isn't a subagent field, so the subagent inherits every tool, and the safety limit you thought you'd set isn't there. Fix: rename the key to tools.

5. A Bash specifier that removes all of Bash

disallowedTools: Bash(rm *) takes away the whole Bash tool, so test runs fail too. Fix: move the pattern to permissions.deny in .claude/settings.json.

6. Too many tools on a read-only job

For example, a "reviewer" with inherited Bash and Write might run a formatter or rewrite files while it reviews. In acceptEdits or auto mode, nothing asks you first. Fix: use an explicit read-only list, and add a hook (next sections) that denies writes from that agent type. For broader rule sets you can paste in, see /ai-agent-guardrails-example-copy-paste-claude-code-rules/.

7. A new MCP server reaches every inheriting agent

Connect a Slack server, and every subagent without a tools list can now post messages. Fix: add disallowedTools: mcp__* to agents that should stay local, or define the server inline with mcpServers so only one agent connects to it.

What are Claude Code hooks and how do they relate to subagents?

Claude Code hooks are commands (or HTTP calls, MCP tools, prompts, or agents) that run automatically at fixed lifecycle points. They give you a second layer of enforcement that keeps working even when a subagent's tool list is wrong. The tools field decides what a subagent can try. A hook can inspect each attempt as it happens and block it.

Hooks reach subagents in two ways (sub-agents docs):

  • Session-wide, from settings. Hooks in settings files, managed policy, and plugins all apply inside subagents, so "a PreToolUse hook in settings.json also runs before every tool a subagent uses."
  • Per subagent, from frontmatter. A hooks: block in the agent file runs only while that subagent is active and is removed when it finishes. A Stop hook in frontmatter becomes SubagentStop (hooks reference).

Each hook gets JSON input that includes agent_id and agent_type (the subagent's name), so one settings-level script can apply different rules to different agents. SubagentStart and SubagentStop also accept a matcher on the agent's name. Plugin-scoped names like my-plugin:db-agent contain a colon, which makes them regex, so anchor them as ^my-plugin:db-agent$.

Example frontmatter hook, adapted from the docs:

---
name: db-migrator
description: Runs database migrations
tools: Read, Bash
hooks:
  PreToolUse:
    - matcher: "Bash"
      hooks:
        - type: command
          command: "./scripts/security-check.sh"
---

For a full map of every event and when it fires, see /claude-code-hooks-lifecycle-every-event-explained/.

What do Claude Code hooks PreToolUse, PostToolUse, UserPromptSubmit, and Notification do?

In Claude Code, PreToolUse runs before a tool call and can block it, and PostToolUse runs after the tool succeeds. UserPromptSubmit runs when a prompt is submitted. Notification runs when Claude Code sends a notification and is for side effects only.

EventWhen it firesMatcher filters onCan it block?Typical subagent use
PreToolUseBefore a tool executesTool name (Bash, `Edit\Write, mcp__memory__.*`)Yes: exit code 2, or permissionDecision: "deny"Deny writes from a reviewer agent
PostToolUseAfter a tool succeedsTool nameNot the tool, which already ran. decision: "block" stops Claude from continuingRun a linter after a subagent edits
UserPromptSubmitWhen a prompt is submitted, before Claude processes itNo matcher; fires every timeYes: exit code 2 or decision: "block"Add project context to every turn
NotificationWhen Claude Code sends a notificationpermission_prompt, idle_prompt, auth_success, agent_needs_input, agent_completed, and othersNo, exit code is ignoredAlert you when an unattended run needs input

All four come from the hooks reference (as of October 2026). A few more details:

  • PreToolUse decisions: permissionDecision accepts "allow", "deny", "ask", or "defer". updatedInput can rewrite the tool's arguments before they run, and additionalContext passes a note to Claude.
  • PostToolUse: updatedToolOutput can replace what the tool returned.
  • UserPromptSubmit also fires on turns Claude Code starts by itself, which matters for automations.
  • Default timeouts: 600 seconds for command, HTTP, and MCP tool hooks, 30 for prompt hooks, and 60 for agent hooks.

Exit codes work like this. 0 means success, and any JSON output is applied. 2 is a blocking error on events that can block. Any other code is a non-blocking error, and the action goes ahead unless you set onFailure: "block". For ready-made scripts on these events, see /claude-code-hooks-examples-7-copy-paste-scripts/.

What is a Claude Code hook and how do you configure one?

A Claude Code hook is a JSON settings entry that runs a handler when an event matches. The handler is usually a shell command, and the entry links it to an event and a matcher. Here is how to set up a hook that stops a read-only subagent from writing files, even if its tool list was set up wrong.

Steps

  1. Choose the scope. .claude/settings.json is for one project and is shared through git. .claude/settings.local.json is for one project and is gitignored. ~/.claude/settings.json covers all your projects (hooks reference).
  2. Create the script at .claude/hooks/deny-reviewer-writes.sh (example):
#!/bin/bash
INPUT=$(cat)
AGENT=$(echo "$INPUT" | jq -r '.agent_type // empty')

if [ "$AGENT" = "code-reviewer" ]; then
  jq -n '{
    hookSpecificOutput: {
      hookEventName: "PreToolUse",
      permissionDecision: "deny",
      permissionDecisionReason: "code-reviewer is read-only"
    }
  }'
else
  exit 0
fi
  1. Make it executable: chmod +x .claude/hooks/deny-reviewer-writes.sh. You also need jq installed.
  2. Register it in .claude/settings.json:
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Edit|Write|NotebookEdit",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/.claude/hooks/deny-reviewer-writes.sh"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
  1. Open /hooks in a session to confirm the hook is listed and to see which file it came from.
  2. Run the reviewer on a small diff and ask it to fix something. The write attempt should come back denied, with your reason.

Matcher rules to get right

A matcher that is "", "", or left out matches everything. A value made only of letters, digits, _, -, spaces, , and | is treated as an exact name or a list. Anything else is treated as an unanchored JavaScript regex (hooks reference). So mcp__github__. is a regex that covers every GitHub MCP tool. You can narrow further with the if field, which takes permission-rule syntax such as "Bash(rm *)".

Common mistakes and fixes

  • Script paths relative to cwd break in worktrees. Use ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}. In worktrees it stays at the main checkout, while cwd points to the worktree.
  • Checking tool_name == "Task". Since v2.1.63 the name is Agent (issue #29677).
  • Expecting Notification to block. It can't. Use PreToolUse or a permission rule.
  • A crashing script lets the action through. A non-zero exit other than 2 doesn't block. For security hooks, set "onFailure": "block".
  • Hooks seem to do nothing. Look for "disableAllHooks": true in your settings, or a --settings override in your cron command. Cron wrappers are covered in /claude-code-cron-job-setup-run-automations-overnight/.

Next steps

Do today (DIY):

  1. Search your agents for the wrong key: grep -rn "allowed-tools" .claude/agents ~/.claude/agents. Rename every match to tools.
  2. For each subagent that runs unattended, write out a tools list built only from the background keep-list, then ask the subagent to list its tools before its next real run.
  3. Add one PreToolUse hook like the one above for your most sensitive agent, and put Bash(git push *) in permissions.deny if no agent should push.

If you'd rather not set this up by hand: the main official option is a Claude subscription that includes Claude Code, so you can ask Claude to write and check agent files for you. Claude Pro is $20/month ($17/month billed annually), and Max starts at $100/month with 5x or 20x Pro's usage (as of October 2026; check the official pricing page). Pro suits solo builders running a few scheduled subagents. Max suits people who run many parallel or long jobs and keep hitting limits. Neither plan reviews your configuration for you, and the Free plan doesn't include Claude Code. If your runs are small and occasional, pay-as-you-go API use may cost less. Token tracking is covered in /claude-code-how-to-see-token-usage-and-reduce-it/.

  • /claude-code-permissions-best-practices-headless-template/

FAQ

What tools can a Claude Code subagent use?

If you don't set a tools field, it inherits the main conversation's built-in and MCP tools, minus a few that are always withheld, such as AskUserQuestion and EnterPlanMode. Background subagents, the default, keep only a fixed set of built-ins like Read, Edit, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob, WebFetch, and WebSearch, plus all MCP tools. Use tools or disallowedTools to narrow that set.

What are Claude Code hooks?

Hooks are handlers you configure in settings files or agent frontmatter, usually shell commands, that run automatically at lifecycle events such as PreToolUse, PostToolUse, SessionStart, and SubagentStop. They get JSON describing the event and can allow, deny, or change some actions. Hooks set in settings also run inside subagents.

Where are the docs for PreToolUse, PostToolUse, UserPromptSubmit, and Notification?

All four are on the official hooks reference, with input fields, matcher values, and decision options for each. The sub-agents page covers how those events behave inside subagents and the SubagentStart/SubagentStop matchers.

How do I make a Claude Code hook block a command?

Register a PreToolUse hook with a matcher such as Bash, and either exit with code 2 or print JSON with permissionDecision: "deny" and a reason. Add "onFailure": "block" if a crashing script should also block. For simple command patterns, a permissions.deny rule is often enough and needs no script.

item.title: AI Agent vs Automation: A 5-Question Test for Claude Code
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: AI agent vs automation, settled with a 5-question test: when a Claude Code agent is worth its cost and when a plain script or cron job is the better choice.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

The difference between an AI agent and automation comes down to who picks the next step. With automation, you write every step ahead of time and the same input always takes the same path. With an AI agent such as Claude Code, the model looks at the situation and chooses its own next action. Anthropic's engineering guide puts it this way: workflows are systems "orchestrated through predefined code paths," and agents are systems "where LLMs dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage" (Anthropic, Building Effective Agents). Here is the practical test. If a task needs judgment at points where the right path depends on messy input, use an agent at those points. If the task is just steps on predictable input, write a script.

Which option is right for you?

Most solo builders should start with a script. Add a Claude Code agent step only where the script keeps failing on inputs it can't predict.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner, never automated anythingA plain shell script or cron job. You can read every line, and debugging is easyClaude Code Cron Job Setup
Daily dev work (PR reviews, failing tests, triage)A Claude Code agent in headless mode (claude -p) with a short tool allowlistRun Claude Code programmatically
Work that lives on GitHub (issues, PRs)The Claude Code GitHub Action, triggered by @claude or a scheduleClaude Code GitHub Actions
Tight budget, fixed and structured inputsA script, with no model calls. Each run costs nothing beyond computeMake: when to use AI agents
Mostly fixed steps plus one fuzzy decisionA hybrid: script around a single claude -p --json-schema callThe "How do you combine both?" section below
Unattended runs overnightA headless agent with strict permissions and retry handlingPermissions headless template

One reason for each pick. Scripts fail loudly and in the same place every time, so they suit beginners. Agents are worth their cost when inputs vary, as with diffs, logs and tickets. The GitHub Action saves you from writing your own server. A hybrid keeps the model's freedom limited to one step.

What Is the Difference Between AI Agent and Automation?

Automation runs steps you defined in advance. An AI agent like Claude Code decides which steps to run, based on what it observes as it works.

Under the hood, Anthropic describes the building block of agentic systems as an LLM enhanced with retrieval, tools and memory (Building Effective Agents). Claude Code is that building block packaged as a tool. It reads files, runs shell commands, edits code, and loops until it decides the job is finished. A cron job that runs rsync never decides anything. It does exactly what the line says.

Scripted automationAI agent (e.g. Claude Code)
Who chooses the next stepYou, in codeThe model, at runtime
Same input → same output?YesNot guaranteed
Handles inputs you didn't anticipateNo, it errors or does the wrong thing silentlyOften, by reasoning about them
Cost per runCompute onlyModel tokens plus compute (--output-format json reports total_cost_usd, per the headless docs)
SpeedMilliseconds to secondsSeconds to minutes
Failure modeCrash at a known linePlausible but wrong action, or errors that compound
DebuggingRead the codeRead the transcript

For example, a script that moves invoices from an inbox to a folder works perfectly until a vendor sends a PDF named scan001.pdf with no invoice number in the subject line. An agent can open the PDF, find the number, and file it. It can also misread it. Both outcomes are possible, and that is the trade.

Anthropic is direct about the cost: "agentic systems often trade latency and cost for better task performance" (Building Effective Agents). The same article warns about the "potential for compounding errors" in autonomous runs, which is why agents need guardrails that scripts don't.

AI Agent vs Automation Workflow: Which One Fits Your Task?

A task needs a Claude Code agent when it requires branching judgment on varied or unstructured input. If it only needs repeatable steps on structured input, a script fits better.

Here are the five questions. Answer them for one specific recurring task, not for "my work" in general.

  1. Can you write the steps down completely today? If yes, and they cover at least nine out of ten real cases, write a script. If you keep writing "it depends", that is where judgment lives.
  2. Is the input structured? JSON from an API, a CSV with fixed columns, and a database row are structured. A bug report, a stack trace, a git diff or a customer email is not. Unstructured input points toward an agent.
  3. Does the number of steps vary? Anthropic recommends agents for "open-ended problems where it's difficult or impossible to predict the required number of steps" (Building Effective Agents). Fixing a failing test might take one edit or twelve. Syncing two APIs always takes the same calls.
  4. What does a wrong answer cost? If a mistake is cheap and reversible, such as a draft comment or a label, an agent is fine. If it is expensive or permanent, such as a payment, a deleted record or a production deploy, keep that step scripted, or let the agent only propose and have a human approve.
  5. Does it run often enough that the cost per run matters? A job that runs every 5 minutes pays model costs 288 times a day. If a script can do it, the script wins on budget.

How to score it: two or more answers that point to an agent (no to Q1, unstructured for Q2, variable for Q3) means an agent step is justified. A high-cost answer on Q4 means that step stays scripted or gated, whatever the other answers say.

Example, labeled as an illustration. "Every morning, check the CI failures from last night and open a fix PR." Q1: no, because every failure is different. Q2: unstructured logs. Q3: variable. Q4: medium, since a PR is reviewable before merge. Q5: once a day. The result is an agent, with the PR as the human checkpoint. Compare "Every morning, back up the Postgres database to S3." Q1: yes. Q2: structured. Q3: fixed. Q4: high. The result is a script.

Common mistake: running the test on the whole pipeline instead of on each step. "Triage support tickets" fails the test as one unit. Split it into fetch, classify, route and reply, and usually only "classify" needs an agent.

AI Agent vs Agentic AI vs Automation: How Do the Terms Relate?

Automation is the umbrella. An AI agent such as Claude Code is one kind of automation that makes decisions. "Agentic AI" describes systems built from agent-like parts.

Anthropic's own vocabulary is the clearest anchor. Its guide says "we categorize all these variations as agentic systems," then splits them into workflows and agents (Building Effective Agents). So in Anthropic's usage, "agentic" covers both LLM workflows (fixed code paths that call a model) and true agents (the model directs the path).

TermWhat it means in practiceExample
AutomationAny process that replaces manual work, AI or notCron + bash backup, a Zapier zap, an RPA bot
LLM workflowFixed code path with model calls at defined stepsScript that sends each ticket to Claude for a label, then routes by label
AI agentModel decides its own steps and tool use in a loopclaude -p "Run the test suite and fix any failures"
Agentic AI / agentic systemUmbrella for the two above, and for multi-agent setups such as an orchestrator with workersClaude Code spawning subagents for parallel research

Vendors stretch these words. Some product pages call any chatbot with a webhook "agentic AI". When you see the term, ask one question: who chooses the next step, the code or the model? That answer tells you more than the label does.

Is AI Part of Automation, or Separate From It?

AI is one way to automate, and Claude Code is one AI tool among several. Automation is the goal, and AI, scripting and RPA are methods for reaching it.

The methods sit side by side:

  • Rule-based scripting: bash, Python, cron, CI pipelines. You write every rule yourself.
  • RPA (robotic process automation): UiPath defines it as software robots that "handle repetitive, rule-based tasks like entering data, moving files, or processing transactions" (UiPath). It is still rules, applied through user interfaces.
  • No-code workflow tools: Zapier, Make and n8n. These are rules you build visually, often with an optional AI step.
  • AI agents: Claude Code, the Agent SDK. The model makes the decisions.

UiPath now describes RPA as "the execution layer" under AI agents (UiPath). That reflects the shape most teams end up with: deterministic tools do the actions, and AI decides which action to take.

For example, think of a solo SaaS founder's weekly churn report. A scheduled script pulls cancellations from Stripe's API, which is plain automation. A Claude call reads the free-text cancellation reasons and groups them into themes, which is AI used inside automation. The script then emails the summary, which is automation again. Calling this either "AI" or "automation" would be only half right.

AI Agent Automation Examples: Which Tasks Need an Agent?

Tasks with varied input need an agent. Claude Code agents beat scripts when the fix depends on what the agent finds, as in debugging, code review, triage and research.

These come straight from the patterns in Anthropic's docs:

  • Fixing failing tests. The headless docs show claude -p "Run the test suite and fix any failures" --allowedTools "Bash,Read,Edit" (headless docs). No script can know ahead of time which file to edit.
  • Explaining build errors. cat build-error.txt | claude -p 'concisely explain the root cause of this build error' > output.txt (headless docs). Error logs are unstructured by nature.
  • Pull request review. The GitHub Action's review workflow posts inline comments on each issue it finds, and it skips drafts and PRs it judges not to need review (GitHub Actions docs). "Judges" is the key word there.
  • Issue-to-PR. Comment @claude fix the TypeError in the user dashboard component on an issue and the Action works on it (GitHub Actions docs).
  • Commit messages from staged changes. The docs scope this with --allowedTools "Bash(git diff ),Bash(git log ),Bash(git status ),Bash(git commit )" (headless docs).

Pitfalls and fixes:

  • The agent stops partway through an unattended run. In -p mode with Claude Code v2.1.302 or later, runs start in Manual mode when nothing sets a permission mode, and a call that needs approval is denied (headless docs). Fix: allowlist exactly the tools the job needs. Why Claude Code stops mid-automation walks through the causes.
  • The agent waits for an approval nobody will give. Add --permission-prompts none (requires v2.1.259 or later). Prompts are then denied and Claude is told not to retry them (headless docs).
  • The agent does too much. Put limits on it: --max-turns, a tool allowlist, and written rules. See the guardrails example.
  • The agent behaves differently on another machine. Use --bare. It skips the hooks, plugins, MCP servers and CLAUDE.md files found on the host. Note that bare mode needs ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and doesn't use your subscription login (headless docs).

Who agents are not for: anyone who needs byte-identical output on every run, such as compliance exports or invoice numbering. Agents also cost money on every run, and that cost varies with codebase size and task complexity (GitHub Actions docs).

AI Automation Examples: Which Tasks Should Stay Scripted?

Backups, syncs between two APIs, templated emails and scheduled reports from fixed queries should stay scripted. They need no judgment, and a script is cheaper, faster and repeatable.

Make's own guidance says it plainly: for jobs like notifications and record updates, "classic automation is faster, cheaper, and easier to maintain" (Make). Make lists the conditions where agents don't fit: rules that are fixed and stable, inputs that are clean and structured, and speed and consistency that matter more than judgment.

Examples where a script is the better tool:

TaskWhy a script wins
Nightly pg_dump to S3Same command every night, and a wrong action is costly
Copy new Stripe customers into your CRMStructured JSON on both ends, with a fixed field mapping
Send a welcome email from a templateNo decision at all
Rotate logs older than 14 daysfind -mtime +14 -delete is one line and has no edge cases
Bump a version and tag a releaseDeterministic, and reproducibility matters

Pitfalls and fixes:

  • Putting a model call into a task that has no decision in it. This adds cost and latency and makes the result less consistent. Fix: delete the model call and see whether anything gets worse.
  • Using a session-scoped /loop for something durable. Recurring /loop tasks expire 7 days after creation and only fire while the session runs (scheduled tasks docs). Fix: use system cron, a Desktop scheduled task, a cloud Routine, or GitHub Actions. Cloud Routines have a 1-hour minimum interval, while Desktop tasks and /loop go down to 1 minute (as of October 2026, per the same page).
  • Assuming GitHub scheduled workflows run forever. In public repositories, GitHub disables a schedule after 60 days without repository activity (GitHub Actions docs). Fix: add a check that alerts you when a run is missing, or schedule the job on a machine you control.

Who scripts are not for: tasks whose inputs change faster than you can update the rules. If you keep patching regexes for new edge cases every week, that is the sign to move that one step to an agent.

Using AI for Automation: How Do You Combine Both?

Use a hybrid. Scripted automation does the deterministic steps, and a single Claude Code call sits at the one decision point that needs judgment.

Anthropic's guide describes this shape. "Prompt chaining" splits a task into a sequence of steps, and "routing classifies an input and directs it to a specialized followup task" (Building Effective Agents). It lists five workflow patterns in total: prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers and evaluator-optimizer. For solo builders, routing is the most useful one: the model labels the input, and your code acts on the label.

Steps to build one (the example below is an illustration of support-ticket triage):

  1. Write the deterministic parts first. Fetch the input and save it to a file. Piped stdin to claude -p is capped at 10MB, and for anything bigger the docs say to write it to a file and reference the path (headless docs).
  2. Make the model return a fixed shape. Use --output-format json with --json-schema. The result arrives in the structured_output field (headless docs). An enum in the schema keeps labels to a closed set your script can branch on.
  3. Give the agent step the fewest tools possible. A classifier needs Read and nothing else.
  4. Branch in code, not in the prompt. jq reads the label, and case decides what happens next.
  5. Check the exit code. Claude Code "exits with code 0 on success and a non-zero code when the run fails" (headless docs).
  6. Schedule it with cron. See Claude Code Cron Job Setup.
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Example: hybrid triage. Script steps around one agent step.
set -euo pipefail

./fetch_new_tickets.sh > /tmp/tickets.json   # deterministic (your own script)

schema='{"type":"object","properties":{"items":{"type":"array","items":{"type":"object","properties":{"id":{"type":"string"},"label":{"type":"string","enum":["refund","bug","other"]}},"required":["id","label"]}}},"required":["items"]}'

out=$(claude --bare -p "Read /tmp/tickets.json. Label each ticket refund, bug, or other." \
  --allowedTools "Read" \
  --output-format json \
  --json-schema "$schema") || { echo "agent step failed" >&2; exit 1; }

echo "$out" | jq -r '.total_cost_usd'          # log spend per run
echo "$out" | jq -c '.structured_output.items[]' | while read -r t; do
  case "$(echo "$t" | jq -r .label)" in
    refund) ./route_to_billing.sh "$t" ;;      # deterministic
    bug)    ./open_issue.sh "$t" ;;            # deterministic
    *)      ./send_template_reply.sh "$t" ;;   # deterministic
  esac
done

Common mistakes with hybrids:

  • Letting the agent take the actions too. If Claude both classifies and issues the refund, you have handed a high-cost Q4 step to the model. Keep actions in your own scripts.
  • Ignoring rate limits. A cron job that hits a limit at 3 a.m. fails silently unless you handle it. The stream emits system/api_retry events with fields like attempt and retry_delay_ms (headless docs). See the rate limit retry setup.
  • Not tracking token spend. total_cost_usd is a client-side estimate and can differ from your bill (headless docs). Log it anyway, and read how to see token usage and reduce it.

AI Agent and Automation Course: Is It Worth Taking One?

You usually don't need a paid course. Anthropic's Claude Code documentation, the Building Effective Agents article and the cookbook cover the core material at no cost.

What the free material covers:

  • Concepts and patterns: Building Effective Agents, published December 19, 2024. It defines workflows and agents and the five patterns.
  • Running agents headless: the headless docs and the GitHub Actions docs, with copy-paste commands and YAML.
  • Code recipes: the anthropics/claude-cookbooks repo, "a collection of notebooks/recipes" that includes tool use and agent examples.
  • Structured lessons: the Anthropic Academy course catalog lists more than 20 courses, including Claude Code 101, Claude Code in Action, Introduction to subagents and Introduction to agent skills. The catalog page doesn't show prices. Third-party roundups describe the courses as free with a certificate (Analytics Vidhya), so confirm on the course page before you enroll.

When a course helps: you learn better with a sequenced curriculum and exercises than by reading reference docs. When it doesn't: you already know the problem you want to solve. Building that one hybrid script teaches you more than a general course will.

Pitfalls when choosing a third-party course: tools change quickly. The headless docs alone mention behavior changes at several 2.1.x versions. A course recorded a year ago may teach flags that have since been renamed. Check the recording date. Be wary of any course that promises income from "AI automation agencies". That promise is about marketing, not about the skill you are trying to learn.

Next steps

Do it yourself today:

  1. Pick one recurring task and run the five-question test on each of its steps. Write the answers down.
  2. If every step comes out "script", write the script and schedule it with cron. You're done, and no model is involved.
  3. If one step comes out "agent", try that step alone first: claude -p "<your instruction>" --allowedTools "Read" --output-format json. Then wrap it with the hybrid script above.

If you'd rather not build it yourself:

  • Claude Pro: $20/month billed monthly, or $17/month with annual billing ($200 up front). Claude Code is included (Claude pricing, as of October 2026; check the official page). It suits a solo builder running a few agent jobs a day. It doesn't suit --bare scripts, which need an API key instead of your subscription login (headless docs).
  • Claude Max: from $100/month, billed monthly (Claude pricing, as of October 2026; check the official page). It suits heavy daily agent use. It is overkill if your agent step runs once a day.
  • Claude Code GitHub Action: no server to run, and setup is /install-github-app (GitHub Actions docs). It suits repo-centric work. It doesn't suit local-only files, and it uses GitHub Actions minutes as well as API tokens or your subscription.
  • Anthropic Academy courses: structured lessons at anthropic.skilljar.com. They suit people who like guided exercises. They won't build your specific pipeline for you.

Related guides on this site:

  • Claude Code Permissions Best Practices: Headless Template
  • Claude Code Checkpoints: How Rollback Works in Automations
  • Claude Code Hooks Examples: 7 Copy-Paste Scripts

FAQ

What is AI agent and automation?

Automation is any setup that does manual work for you by following rules you wrote. An AI agent is a kind of automation where a model such as Claude decides its own next steps and which tools to use, in a loop. You can combine them: scripts for the fixed steps, an agent for the judgment calls.

What is an AI agent vs automation?

A scripted automation takes the same path every time for the same input. An AI agent may take a different path each run, depending on what it finds. Anthropic describes agents as systems where the model maintains "control over how they accomplish tasks" (Building Effective Agents). Choose based on whether the task needs judgment.

AI agents vs automation: what are people saying on Reddit?

This guide doesn't summarize Reddit threads, because forum opinions can't be sourced the way documentation can. When you read them, judge each claim with the five-question test. Ask whether the commenter is describing structured or unstructured input, and whether a wrong action in their case could be undone. Claims about limits or pricing should be checked against the vendor's official page.

Automation vs AI: which term should I use?

Use "automation" for the goal and "AI" for the method. A cron job is automation without AI. A script that calls Claude to classify text is AI-assisted automation. Say "agent" only when the model chooses the steps, which avoids the vague way "agentic" often gets used.
